lessons.rawTitle: Bài 1: Why data people need Git

theory.contentHtml:
Open your project folder: analysis_final_v2_THAT_ONE.ipynb is sitting next to six other copies, and nobody - including you - dares to delete any of them. This lesson is about the tool built to end that scene, and why data people need it every bit as much as software engineers do.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Seven copies of one notebook
  2. What version control is
  3. How Git differs from Google Drive
  4. A commit is a snapshot of the whole project
  5. Git is not GitHub
  6. Command reference
  7. Key points
  8. Practice on your machine

1. Seven copies of one notebook

Does this look familiar:

analysis.ipynb
analysis_v2.ipynb
analysis_final.ipynb
analysis_final_v2.ipynb
analysis_final_FINAL.ipynb
analysis_final_v2_THAT_ONE.ipynb
analysis_old_DO_NOT_DELETE.ipynb

This is manual version control: every time you are afraid of breaking the thing that currently works, you copy the file and edit the new copy. It "works" - until you need to answer a real question:

  • Which copy produced the report you sent your boss last month?
  • What exactly is different between final and final_v2?
  • Can analysis_old_DO_NOT_DELETE be deleted? Nobody knows, so nobody dares.

File names answer none of those three questions. They record neither when you made the copy, why you made it, nor what changed since the previous one. You are storing versions while throwing away the most valuable part: the story between them.

Teamwork makes it worse: you send the notebook over chat, a colleague edits it and sends back analysis_final_v2 (1).ipynb, and now each of you holds your own "latest version". Versioning by file name collapses the moment a second person joins.

2. What version control is

A version control system records a project's history as milestones - each one pins down the state of the project at a moment in time, along with three things the pile of copies above never had: who created it, when, and one line describing why.

In Git, each such milestone is called a commit. The same analysis project from section 1, under Git, has a history that looks like this (printed by git log --oneline - you will run it yourself in the "Your first repo" lesson):

e4f2a10 (HEAD -> main) Fix revenue double counting in March
9c81b3f Add customer churn section
f3a9c21 Add raw sales data and first analysis

One single file analysis.ipynb, no copies left - yet all three questions from section 1 now have answers. Want to know which version produced last month's report: read the history, find the matching milestone, and bring the whole project back to exactly that point. Want to know how two versions differ: Git can compare any two milestones line by line.

Each milestone holds more than that one line. The same command without --oneline shows a commit in full:

commit e4f2a10c9d3b7f215a84d6e0b2f4c8a1d5e6f7a8
Author: An Nguyen <an.nguyen@gmail.com>
Date:   Tue Jul 14 10:32:07 2026 +0700

    Fix revenue double counting in March

Who, when, why - exactly the three answers the pile of copies never had, now recorded automatically on every milestone.

For data people, the value comes down to two very concrete things:

  • Reproducing old results. "How was the number in the June slide computed?" is no longer archaeology - the code that produced it lives at a milestone with a name and a date.
  • Experimenting without fear. Want to try a new way of computing something? Edit away. If it breaks, go back to the last milestone - no more copying files "just in case" before daring to touch anything.

3. How Git differs from Google Drive

A very common question: "Doesn't Drive/Dropbox have version history too?". It does, but the two solve different problems:

+--------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                |            Google Drive / Dropbox           |                             Git                             |
+--------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| When a version is created      | Automatically, every time the file is saved | Deliberately - you decide when a milestone is worth pinning |
| Comes with a description       | No - only a timestamp                       | Yes - every commit carries a one-line message you wrote     |
| Scope                          | Each file separately                        | The whole project in one milestone                          |
| Answers "why did this change?" | No                                          | That is exactly what the commit message is for              |
+--------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------+

Autosave keeps every state, including moments when the code was half-written and broken - so its history is hundreds of near-identical versions, none of them marked "this one actually works". Git is the opposite: between two commits you edit freely, and only when everything runs correctly do you pin a milestone, with a sentence explaining it. Git history is therefore sparse but made entirely of meaningful milestones - a lab notebook, not a surveillance camera.

One concrete situation shows the difference: this afternoon you discover the churn calculation has been wrong since last week. On Drive, you open the notebook's version history and scroll through thirty unnamed autosaves, guessing which one is "before I changed the calculation". With Git, you read the history, spot the Add customer churn section milestone immediately, and know exactly where to look.

The second difference matters even more for data people: Drive restores one file at a time. But the June notebook ran correctly because it sat next to the June version of data/sales.csv. Restore just the notebook after the data changed schema and the result is still wrong. Git brings back the whole project at once - code and sample data return to the same moment together.

4. A commit is a snapshot of the whole project

Beginners often picture this wrong, so let's be blunt: a commit is not a copy of one file, and it is not a list of changed lines. A commit is a snapshot - a photograph of the entire project at that moment: every file, exactly as it was.

commit f3a9c21          commit 9c81b3f          commit e4f2a10
┌────────────────┐      ┌────────────────┐      ┌────────────────┐
│ analysis.ipynb │      │ analysis.ipynb │      │ analysis.ipynb │
│ data/sales.csv │ ───► │ data/sales.csv │ ───► │ data/sales.csv │
│ README.md      │      │ README.md      │      │ README.md      │
└────────────────┘      └────────────────┘      └────────────────┘

Three commits, each box being the complete state of the project - even when you only touched one file between two milestones. That is why "going back to commit f3a9c21" means the whole folder returns to exactly that shape, rather than restoring files one by one and stitching them together by hand.

What about the "diff" - the list of changed lines? Diffs are real, but a diff is something Git computes when you ask it to compare two milestones, not something it stores. The distinction changes how you ask questions: not "what changes does this commit contain" but "what did the project look like at this milestone".

Sounds wasteful - photographing the whole project every time? It isn't: internally, a file that did not change between two milestones is reused, not stored again. Think in snapshots to get the logic right; Git handles the disk-space part for you. For data people, the snapshot is what reproducibility means: reopen the June milestone, run the notebook on the June sample data, get the June numbers - not "roughly".

5. Git is not GitHub

Get this straight early, before the two blur together:

  • Git is software installed on your machine. The entire history lives inside the project folder, and every operation runs fully local - with no internet you can still commit, still read history, still go back to old milestones.
  • GitHub is a web service that hosts a copy of your repo - for backup, sharing, and teamwork. GitLab and Bitbucket are services of the same kind.

It is like photos on your phone and Google Photos: pictures are taken and stored on the device; Photos is where you choose to upload them. Without Photos, the pictures are still on your phone - without GitHub, Git is still fully functional.

The boundary of this course is therefore clear:

  • This module: Git on your machine - committing, reading history, the three areas of a repo.
  • A later module: putting the repo on GitHub - off-machine backup, sharing, teamwork.

The most common mix-up: "committing means pushing code to the internet". Wrong - a commit only records a milestone in the history on your machine. Sending that history to GitHub is a separate step, with different commands, taught in a later module. Throughout this module you work purely locally, no account needed.

Command reference

This is a concepts lesson, so the table is short - it grows from the next lesson on.

+-------------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|      Command      |                                                     What it does                                                     |
+-------------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| git log --oneline | Prints the commit history, one milestone per line: hash + message. Previewed here, run for real in "Your first repo" |
+-------------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Key points

Naming files _final_v2 is manual version control - it stores versions but throws away the most valuable part: when things changed, why, and what differs from the previous copy. Git keeps exactly that part.

A commit is a snapshot of the whole project, not a copy of one file. Going back to a commit returns the entire folder to that moment - code and sample data in sync, which Drive cannot do.

Git runs locally; GitHub is a hosting service. Committing needs no internet and sends nothing anywhere. This module uses Git on your machine only.

Practice on your machine

This lesson has no Git commands yet, so the practice is to observe your own current state and set up the practice area for the lessons that follow.

  1. Open the folder holding your real analysis projects / homework (with a file manager or a terminal) and list the files:
ls

Count how many names look like _v2, _final, copy, _old. Delete nothing - just count. That is the "manual version control" from section 1.

  1. Pick the newest copy among them and try to answer the three questions from section 1 using the file name alone: when was it created, why, and what differs from the previous one? Write your answers on scrap paper - you will find the file name answers none of them.

  2. Create a dedicated practice folder for the whole course - every exercise from now on happens in here, never touching your real projects:

mkdir -p ~/git-practice

The command prints nothing when it finishes - in the terminal, silence usually means success.

  1. Confirm the folder is there:
ls ~

You should see git-practice in the listing.

Self-check:

  • You pointed at least one _final/_v2-style file in a real project (or confirmed you never name files that way).
  • You tried and could not answer "when / why / what changed" from file names alone - exactly the gap a commit (who, when, one message line saying why) fills.
  • ls ~ shows the git-practice folder - ready for "Install Git and introduce yourself".

lessons.title: Install Git and introduce yourself
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 2: Install Git and introduce yourself

theory.contentHtml:
Before creating your first milestone, two things need doing: make sure Git is on the machine, and tell Git who you are - because every commit permanently stamps the name of its author. The whole lesson is exactly five commands, and you do it once per machine.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Check whether Git is already there
  2. Tell Git your name and email
  3. Make main the default branch
  4. Review your configuration
  5. Global scope and per-repo scope
  6. Command reference
  7. Key points
  8. Practice on your machine

1. Check whether Git is already there

Open a terminal (on Windows: Git Bash, see below) and type:

git --version

Output:

git version 2.39.2

Your version number will almost certainly differ - anything from 2.28 up is fine for this course. If you see a git version ... line, you are done; skip to section 2.

If you get command not found:

  • macOS - run xcode-select --install; the OS installs the Command Line Tools, which include Git.
  • Linux (Ubuntu/Debian) - install through the package manager:
sudo apt install git
  • Windows - download Git for Windows from git-scm.com and install with the defaults. The installer ships Git Bash: a terminal that runs every command in this course as-is. On Windows use Git Bash instead of CMD, and git --version will print something like git version 2.39.2.windows.1 - the .windows.1 part is normal.

2. Tell Git your name and email

Every commit permanently records who made it. When a whole team edits one project, the history is what answers "the revenue calculation changed last month - who changed it, so I can ask why?". Git takes that identity from its configuration, so it must be set before your first commit:

git config --global user.name "An Nguyen"
git config --global user.email "an.nguyen@gmail.com"

Substitute your own name and email - keep the double quotes, since names contain spaces. Both commands print nothing on success: with Git, silence means it worked.

What if you skip this step and commit anyway? Git stops and insists:

Author identity unknown

*** Please tell me who you are.

Run

  git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
  git config --global user.name "Your Name"

to set your account's default identity.
Omit --global to set the identity only in this repository.

fatal: unable to auto-detect email address (got 'an@laptop.(none)')

Nothing is broken - set the identity and run the commit again - but setting it first is tidier, and the message above is exactly the two commands you just learned.

Two notes worth money:

  • The email should match your GitHub account (if you have one, or plan to). GitHub identifies your commits by this email - set it differently and later, when you push code, your commits will not count toward your profile and the contribution graph stays blank despite daily work.
  • Write the name without diacritics (An Nguyen rather than An Nguyễn) so it displays consistently in every tool that reads history.

3. Make main the default branch

Run one more command:

git config --global init.defaultBranch main

A branch is a concept covered properly in a later module - for now, think of it as the project's main line of history, and it has a name. The command above names it main for every repo you create from now on.

Why set it? The old default name was master; since Git 2.28 the community has been moving to main, and GitHub also uses main for repos created on the web. Without this setting, depending on your Git version, your local repos may come out with the old name - and once you connect to GitHub you get two sides with two branch names, which takes tedious manual renaming to fix. One command now saves a debugging session later.

4. Review your configuration

Check that all three values landed correctly:

git config --list

Output:

user.name=An Nguyen
user.email=an.nguyen@gmail.com
init.defaultbranch=main

Your machine may print a few extra lines (preset by the installer) - that is fine, as long as these three are present and correct. Note that Git prints key names in lowercase (init.defaultbranch) even though you typed init.defaultBranch - configuration names are case-insensitive.

To read one value instead of the whole list:

git config user.name

Output:

An Nguyen

Got something wrong? Run the same git config --global command again with the new value - a later run overwrites the earlier one, nothing to delete.

5. Global scope and per-repo scope

The --global flag you have been typing has a precise meaning: it writes the setting into the ~/.gitconfig file in your home directory - applying to every repo of yours on this machine. That is why this lesson only has to be done once.

Drop the --global flag and run the command inside a repo, and the setting is written to that repo's own .git/config:

git config user.email "an.nguyen@company.com"

When both places set the same key, the repo's value beats the global value. This handles a very everyday situation: personal email for all your projects, but the company repo uses your work email - step into that one repo, set it once, and no other repo is affected.

Two easy stumbles:

  • Running git config without --global while standing outside any repo fails with fatal: not in a git directory - Git has no .git/config to write to.
  • Changing configuration only affects commits from now on. Commits already created keep the identity they were born with - history does not rewrite itself.

Command reference

+------------------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        Command                       |                                   What it does                                  |
+------------------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| git --version                                        | Checks whether Git is installed and which version it is                         |
| git config --global user.name "An Nguyen"            | Sets the author name for all future commits, in every repo on the machine       |
| git config --global user.email "an.nguyen@gmail.com" | Sets the author email - should match your GitHub email                          |
| git config --global init.defaultBranch main          | New repos from now on use a default branch named main                           |
| git config --list                                    | Prints every setting currently in effect                                        |
| git config user.name                                 | Reads one specific configuration value                                          |
| git config user.email "an@company.com"               | Without --global: applies only to the current repo, overriding the global value |
+------------------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Key points

--global configuration is done once per machine. It lives in ~/.gitconfig and every repo shares it; got a value wrong, run the command again with the new value and it overwrites.

Your Git email should match your GitHub email. That is how GitHub identifies your commits - a mismatch causes no error today, but later your contributions will not be counted, and fixing old history is far more painful than setting it right from the start.

Repo config beats global config, and only affects future commits. Commits already created keep the identity they were born with - one more reason to set it correctly before your first commit, which is the next lesson's job.

Practice on your machine

Run the lesson's five commands, in order, on your own machine - done once, they serve every repo from now on.

  1. Open a terminal (Windows: Git Bash) and check Git:
git --version

You should see a git version ... line with a number of 2.28 or higher. If you get command not found, install following section 1 and run it again.

  1. Set your name and email - substitute your own values (email matching your GitHub email if you have one, name without diacritics, keep the double quotes):
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

Both commands print nothing - silence means success.

  1. Set the default branch:
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
  1. Review the whole configuration:
git config --list

The list must contain user.name=... and user.email=... with the values you just set, plus init.defaultbranch=main (Git prints key names in lowercase - that is normal).

  1. Read one single value:
git config user.name

It must print exactly the name you set. Got something wrong? Run the matching --global command again with the new value - a later run overwrites the earlier one.

Self-check:

  • git --version prints a version number of 2.28 or higher.
  • git config --list shows all three lines user.name / user.email / init.defaultbranch=main, with the email matching your GitHub email.
  • The git config --global ... commands printed nothing when run - exactly the success signal the lesson taught.

lessons.title: Your first repo init, add, commit
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 3: Your first repo init, add, commit

theory.contentHtml:
Identity set - now for the real thing: build a small analysis project, turn it into a Git repo, and create your first two commits. Along the way you will meet the most important concept of the entire course - the three areas every change passes through in order.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. The sales-analysis sample project
  2. git init creates the .git folder
  3. The three areas of a repo
  4. add, then commit
  5. Reading history with git log
  6. Command reference
  7. Key points
  8. Practice on your machine

1. The sales-analysis sample project

Create the project folder and step inside:

mkdir sales-analysis
cd sales-analysis

Inside it, set up three files every analysis project recognizes - a notebook, a data file, and a description file (create them with any tool you like: VS Code, Jupyter, or the touch command):

sales-analysis/
├── README.md
├── analysis.ipynb
└── data/
    └── sales.csv

At this point it is just an ordinary folder. Git knows nothing about it.

2. git init creates the .git folder

Standing inside sales-analysis, run:

git init

Output:

Initialized empty Git repository in /home/an/sales-analysis/.git/

Read that line carefully: Git just created a hidden folder named .git inside the project. The entire history - every commit, every repo-specific setting - will live inside that .git. Three things follow immediately:

  • A repo = an ordinary folder + .git. No server, no signup - one command, run exactly once per project.
  • Deleting .git deletes the entire history, even though your working files remain intact. The reverse is also useful: to "un-Git" a project, deleting .git is all it takes.
  • Only init at the project's root folder. Accidentally running git init in your home directory turns your whole home into a repo, with Git eyeing every personal file you own - the most common beginner mistake. If it happens, delete the freshly created .git and start over.

3. The three areas of a repo

Before the first commit, you must understand the path a change travels. In Git it passes through three areas:

working directory   --git add-->   staging area   --git commit-->   history
(files you edit)                  (selected, awaiting commit)     (permanent snapshots)
  • Working directory - the real files on disk, the ones you open and edit every day.
  • Staging area - the list of changes you have selected for the next commit.
  • History - the permanent chain of commits, living inside .git.

Why a middle area - why not commit directly? Because committing is an act of selection. A real working session is rarely tidy: you edited the notebook, scribbled in scratch.py, and the notebook spat out a pile of output files. Staging lets you pick exactly what deserves to enter history - the notebook that runs correctly - and leave the junk outside. Without it, every commit is a photo of the whole messy desk, drafts and litter included.

See how Git currently views the project:

git status

Output:

On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	README.md
	analysis.ipynb
	data/

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)

Untracked = the file sits in the folder but Git is not following it yet - it has entered no area at all. Notice the first line too: On branch main - the init.defaultBranch setting from the previous lesson has taken effect.

4. add, then commit

git add moves changes into staging. Try selecting one file first:

git add README.md
git status

Output:

On branch main

No commits yet

Changes to be committed:
  (use "git rm --cached <file>..." to unstage)
	new file:   README.md

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	analysis.ipynb
	data/

The picture splits cleanly in two: README.md has entered staging (Changes to be committed), while the other two paths still stand outside. That is exactly the power of selection from section 3.

This time we do want all three files in the commit, so gather the rest. git add . means "every change from the current folder down":

git add .

Convenient - but precisely because it sweeps everything, it also picks up files you never meant to include. The good habit is to run git status and scan the list before any add ..

Now pin the milestone. -m is the message - the line that will stand next to this commit forever:

git commit -m "Add raw sales data and first analysis"

Output:

[main (root-commit) f3a9c21] Add raw sales data and first analysis
 3 files changed, 128 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 README.md
 create mode 100644 analysis.ipynb
 create mode 100644 data/sales.csv

Read the first line: the commit sits on branch main, is the repo's very first commit (root-commit), and carries the id f3a9c21. Write messages in English, present tense, saying clearly what the milestone contains - "update", "fix bug", "abc" are the messages that make history useless at exactly the moment you need it.

5. Reading history with git log

One commit does not make a "history" yet. Open analysis.ipynb, add a revenue-by-region chart, save, then ask Git:

git status

Output:

On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
	modified:   analysis.ipynb

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")

A new state: modified - the file is tracked, with changes not yet staged. The familiar loop repeats:

git add .
git commit -m "Add revenue by region chart"

Output:

[main a1b2c3d] Add revenue by region chart
 1 file changed, 42 insertions(+), 3 deletions(-)

And now the payoff - the command promised since the first lesson:

git log --oneline

Output:

a1b2c3d (HEAD -> main) Add revenue by region chart
f3a9c21 Add raw sales data and first analysis

Newest on top. Each line starts with a hash - the commit's unique identifier, long enough to never collide, with --oneline showing only the first 7 characters for brevity. The hashes on your machine will definitely differ from the lesson's - a hash is computed from the content, the author, and the moment of the commit, so no two machines match. That is not a mistake. As for HEAD -> main, it marks where you currently stand - a story for the branching module.

From now on, every working session has a rhythm: edit → status → add → commit with a decent message. That rhythm is 90% of the Git you will use daily.

Command reference

+------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|               Command              |                                           What it does                                          |
+------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| git init                           | Turns the current folder into a repo - creates .git, run once per project                       |
| git status                         | Shows which files are untracked / staged / modified - the command to type before every decision |
| git add README.md                  | Moves one specific file's changes into staging                                                  |
| git add .                          | Moves every change from the current folder down into staging                                    |
| git commit -m "Add raw sales data" | Pins whatever is in staging as one commit, with a message                                       |
| git log --oneline                  | Shows the commit history, one milestone per line: hash + message, newest on top                 |
+------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Key points

Every change travels through three areas: working directory → staging → history. Staging exists so that committing is an act of selection - pick exactly what deserves saving, leave drafts and junk behind - rather than a photo of the whole messy desk.

git status is the command you will type most in your life. Before add ., before commit, whenever you forget where you were - type it first. Nothing in this lesson can break anything once you have looked at status first.

A repo is just a folder with .git inside. Delete .git and the history is gone while the files remain; and never git init outside the project's root folder - especially not in your home directory.

Your hashes differ from the lesson's - that is correct. A hash is computed from content, author, and timestamp; all that needs to match is the message and the file counts for what you did.

Practice on your machine

Rebuild the lesson's sales-analysis repo inside the practice folder ~/git-practice (created in "Why data people need Git") and make your first two commits with your own hands.

  1. Create the project folder inside the practice area and step in:
mkdir -p ~/git-practice/sales-analysis
cd ~/git-practice/sales-analysis
  1. Set up the project's three familiar files:
mkdir -p data
touch README.md analysis.ipynb data/sales.csv
  1. Turn the folder into a repo:
git init

You should see Initialized empty Git repository in .../git-practice/sales-analysis/.git/.

  1. Ask Git what it sees:
git status

You should see On branch main (the previous lesson's setting has taken effect), No commits yet, and the three paths README.md / analysis.ipynb / data/ under Untracked files.

  1. Stage one file first, to see the two areas split:
git add README.md
git status

README.md must sit under Changes to be committed, while the other two paths remain under Untracked files - exactly the picture from the lesson's section 4.

  1. Gather the rest and pin the first commit:
git add .
git commit -m "Add raw sales data and first analysis"

The output's first line must contain [main (root-commit) ...] and 3 files changed - your hash differs from the lesson's, and that is correct.

  1. Edit a file, then repeat the add → commit loop:
echo "Revenue analysis for Q3" >> README.md
git status

README.md now shows as modified under Changes not staged for commit. Pin the next milestone:

git add .
git commit -m "Add project description to README"
  1. Read the payoff:
git status
git log --oneline

git status must report nothing to commit, working tree clean; git log --oneline prints exactly two lines, newest commit on top with (HEAD -> main).

Self-check:

  • The final git status reports nothing to commit, working tree clean - every change has entered history.
  • git log --oneline shows exactly 2 commits: Add project description to README on top, Add raw sales data and first analysis below.
  • Both hashes on your machine differ from the lesson's - as the lesson explained, that is the correct sign, not a mistake.
  • The repo lives entirely inside ~/git-practice/sales-analysis, touching no real project of yours.

practice.summaryHtml: You have just run git init for the sales-analysis project. In this exercise you commit each of the two files separately.

sections.title: Scenario
sections.html: The repo has no commits yet. README.md and analysis.ipynb are untracked - run git status to see them.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.html:
• Commit README.md on its own: git add README.md, then git commit -m "...".
  • Commit analysis.ipynb on its own after that. Do not lump the two files into one commit.
  • Finish with a clean working tree: git status says nothing to commit.
  • Write commit messages in English, imperative mood (e.g. add readme).

sections.title: Sandbox
sections.html:
• Type commands into the terminal; the commit graph and Working tree panel update after every command.
  • Besides git you also have edit <file> <content>, cat <file>, ls.

lessons.title: Quiz Getting started with Git
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 6: Quiz Getting started with Git

questions.prompt: What does a Git commit store?

options.label: A
options.text: The list of lines changed since the previous commit

options.label: B
options.text: A snapshot of the entire project's state at the moment of the commit

options.label: C
options.text: A copy of only the files that were just git add-ed

options.label: D
options.text: A compressed archive of the project sent to GitHub

questions.explanation: A commit is a snapshot - a photograph of every file in the project at one moment, including files unchanged since the previous milestone. That is why "going back to an old commit" returns the whole folder to exactly that shape, code and sample data in sync. It is not a list of changed lines (a) - Git can *display* the diff between two commits, but that is computed on comparison, not what a commit stores. Nor is it a copy of just the added files (c): git add selects which changes enter the next milestone, but the milestone itself still photographs the whole project. And nothing goes to GitHub (d) - committing is a purely local operation; sending history online is a separate step with different commands. Disk space is no worry either: a file unchanged between two milestones is reused, not stored again.

questions.prompt: Why does the staging area exist? Why not commit straight from the working directory?

options.label: A
options.text: So Git can automatically back files up before a commit, in case the commit fails

options.label: B
options.text: So you can select exactly which changes go into the next commit, instead of photographing the whole messy desk

options.label: C
options.text: It is where Git stores the project's permanent history

options.label: D
options.text: To speed up commits in projects with many files

questions.explanation: A real working session is rarely tidy: the notebook that runs correctly sits among draft files and temporary output. Staging is the selection step between "files on disk" and "permanent history": git add picks exactly what deserves to enter the next milestone, and the rest stays outside. Without it, every commit would mix in drafts and junk. It is not a backup (a) - changes you have not added get no protection from Git at all. Nor is it where history is stored (c): the permanent history is the chain of commits inside .git, while staging is just the waiting list, considered settled after each commit. And it has nothing to do with speed (d) - the problem staging solves is *what to include*, not *how fast*.

questions.prompt: Your machine has completely lost internet access. Which statement about Git and GitHub is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: You cannot commit, because committing sends data to GitHub

options.label: B
options.text: You can commit but cannot view history, because the history lives on GitHub

options.label: C
options.text: Committing, viewing history, going back to old milestones - everything still works, because Git is a local tool and GitHub only hosts a copy of the repo

options.label: D
options.text: Git stops working, because Git is a GitHub product

questions.explanation: Git is software running on your machine, and the entire history lives in the .git folder right inside the project - so everything in this module works fully offline. GitHub is a web service that *hosts* a copy of the repo for backup and teamwork; it is where you choose to send history, not where history lives. Hence (a) is wrong - "committing means pushing code online" is the single most common misconception; (b) is wrong because the history is in .git on your machine; (d) is wrong because Git was born in 2005, before GitHub, and is independent open-source software - GitHub is just one hosting service among several (alongside GitLab, Bitbucket).

questions.prompt: You run git config --global user.email "an.nguyen@gmail.com". What does this affect?

options.label: A
options.text: Only the repo you were standing in when you ran the command uses this email

options.label: B
options.text: Commits created earlier are updated to the new email

options.label: C
options.text: Your GitHub account's email is changed accordingly

options.label: D
options.text: Every repo of yours on this machine uses that email for commits from now on - except any repo that sets its own value to override it

questions.explanation: The --global flag writes the setting into ~/.gitconfig in your home directory, applying to every repo on the machine - so (a) is wrong; to configure a single repo, drop --global and run the command inside that repo, and the repo's value (in .git/config) overrides the global one. The time direction matters too: configuration only affects commits from now on - commits already created keep the identity they were born with, so (b) is wrong, and this is precisely why you set it correctly before your first commit. And (c) confuses scope: git config only writes to configuration files on your machine and never touches your GitHub account - the real relationship is that you *should set the email to match GitHub* so commits count toward your profile, not that Git can change anything on GitHub.

questions.prompt: The project already lives in Google Drive, and Drive has version history. Why do you still need Git?

options.label: A
options.text: Because Drive cannot store notebook and csv files

options.label: B
options.text: Because Drive cannot restore old versions of a file

options.label: C
options.text: Because Drive's history is per-file autosave - no deliberate milestones with a description for the whole project, and no way to bring the whole project back to one moment

options.label: D
options.text: Because Drive has storage limits and Git does not

questions.explanation: Drive stores any file type (a is wrong) and can restore old versions (b is wrong) - but it solves a different problem. Drive's history is autosave: the machine snapshots every time a file is saved, including moments when the code was half-written and broken, so you get hundreds of near-identical versions with none marked "this one produced the June report". Git is the opposite: you decide when a milestone is worth pinning and write one line explaining why - a history that is sparse but made entirely of meaningful milestones. The second, fatal point for data people: Drive restores *one file at a time*, while the June notebook only ran correctly next to the June data - Git brings the whole project back to one moment, code and data in sync. As for (d), storage limits are not the essential difference between the two tools.

questions.prompt:
You are inside the sales-analysis repo (which already has earlier commits) and git status prints:


On branch main
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
	modified:   analysis.ipynb

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	scratch.py


If you run git commit -m "Update analysis" right now, what will the commit contain?

options.label: A
options.text: Both analysis.ipynb and scratch.py - a commit always photographs every file present in the folder

options.label: B
options.text: Only the changes to analysis.ipynb - the one thing currently in staging; scratch.py stays outside history

options.label: C
options.text: Only scratch.py - new files always take priority over edited files in a commit

options.label: D
options.text: The commit fails - Git refuses to run while untracked files remain

questions.explanation: Read git status through the three areas: Changes to be committed is the staging list - what git commit will pin - and here it holds only analysis.ipynb, so (b) is correct. scratch.py sits under Untracked files: never git add-ed, in no area at all, so it cannot enter the commit - (a) is wrong because a commit does not sweep the folder; it pins only what you selected via add, which is exactly the power of selection staging exists to give you. (c) is wrong because Git has no notion of "new files take priority" - untracked means *not followed*, even further from history than a modified file. (d) is wrong because untracked files never block a commit: Git merely lists them so you know they exist; a commit only fails when staging is empty. The git restore --staged hint in the output is worth noticing too - it is the command that pulls a file back out of staging if you added it by mistake.

questions.prompt:
In the sales-analysis repo, you just edited the data file and git status prints:


On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
	modified:   data/sales.csv

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")


You want this change to become a commit with the message "Update May sales". What is the correct way?

options.label: A
options.text: Run git commit -m "Update May sales" right away - a modified file gets picked up by the commit automatically

options.label: B
options.text: git add data/sales.csv, then git commit -m "Update May sales" - move the change into staging first, then pin the milestone

options.label: C
options.text: git add data/sales.csv is enough - after the add, Git creates the commit by itself

options.label: D
options.text: You must run git init first, because "not staged" means the repo has not been initialized

questions.explanation: modified under Changes not staged for commit means: the file is tracked, and the change so far lives only in the working directory - it has not passed through staging. The mandatory path is working directory → staging → history, so you git add and then git commit (b). Committing right away (a) pins nothing: the output says it outright - no changes added to commit - and Git just reprints the status without creating any milestone. (The hint does mention git commit -a - a shortcut that auto-adds *tracked* files before committing - but that is not the bare commit in option (a).) (c) stops halfway: add only puts the change on the waiting list; without commit, nothing has entered permanent history. (d) misreads the message: "not staged" describes where the *change* is, not the state of the repo - the repo must already be initialized for On branch main to print at all; git init runs exactly once per project.

lessons.title: Reading repo state status, diff, log
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 7: Reading repo state status, diff, log

theory.contentHtml:
Opening a repo after a night away, the first question is always: what was I in the middle of? Git answers with three commands - status tells you what is changing, diff tells you exactly how, and log tells you what happened before. Master these three and you will never commit blind again.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. git status - the state map
  2. git diff - exactly what changed
  3. Reading diff output
  4. git log - the project history
  5. Command reference
  6. Key points
  7. Practice on your machine

1. git status - the state map

git status is the command you will type most often all day - before adding, before committing, and any time something feels off. Throughout this lesson we use the repo sales-analysis/ with three files: analysis.ipynb, data/sales.csv and src/clean.py.

Say you have just edited two files and staged one of them:

git status

Output:

On branch main
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
        modified:   src/clean.py

Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
        modified:   analysis.ipynb

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        data/sales.csv

The output splits into exactly three compartments, read bottom-up by how close each is to a commit:

  • Untracked files - files Git has never met. data/sales.csv was just dropped into the folder; Git sees that it exists but is not tracking its content. It stays here until you git add it (start tracking) or list it in .gitignore (next lesson).
  • Changes not staged for commit - tracked files that were just edited, but whose edits are not yet queued for the next commit. analysis.ipynb belongs here.
  • Changes to be committed - edits that are staged: run git commit right now and exactly these lines get written into history. src/clean.py is standing here.

Notice that Git prints the escape hatch for each compartment right in the output - git restore --staged to unstage, git restore to discard. status output is self-documenting; reading it carefully beats asking around.

When everything is committed cleanly:

git status

Output:

On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean

The line working tree clean is the safest state in Git: everything on disk matches the last commit, and whatever you do next, nothing can be lost.

2. git diff - exactly what changed

status only says which files changed. To see which lines, use diff - and this is where newcomers get confused most:

git diff

git diff with no arguments compares the working directory with the staging area - it only shows edits that are not yet git add-ed.

git diff --staged

git diff --staged compares the staging area with the last commit - it shows what is about to be committed.

The classic source of confusion follows directly: edit a file, git add it, then type git diff and see nothing at all. The edits are not lost - they just moved into the zone that git diff --staged covers. The two commands look into two different gaps:

working directory  --git diff-->  staging area  --git diff --staged-->  last commit

A habit worth keeping: run git diff --staged right before every commit. It is the last time you see exactly what you are about to write into history - catching the temporarily hardcoded number, the forgotten debug print, or the absolute path that only exists on your machine.

3. Reading diff output

Change one line in src/clean.py and look at the diff:

git diff src/clean.py

Output:

diff --git a/src/clean.py b/src/clean.py
index 3f2a8b1..9c4d7e2 100644
--- a/src/clean.py
+++ b/src/clean.py
@@ -4,5 +4,5 @@ import pandas as pd

 def load_sales(path):
     df = pd.read_csv(path)
-    df = df.dropna()
+    df = df.dropna(subset=["revenue"])
     return df

Layer by layer:

  • --- a/src/clean.py and +++ b/src/clean.py - a/ is the old version, b/ the new one. Same name on both sides means an in-place edit, not a rename.
  • @@ -4,5 +4,5 @@ - the hunk header: the changed region starts at line 4 and spans 5 lines, in both the old version (-4,5) and the new one (+4,5). The text after it (import pandas as pd) is the nearest landmark so you can orient yourself by eye.
  • Lines starting with - - present in the old version, removed. Lines starting with + - added. A modified line shows up as an adjacent -/+ pair, as above: dropna() sweeping every column is replaced by dropna(subset=["revenue"]) sweeping only the revenue column.
  • Lines with no marker - surrounding context, unchanged, printed so you know where you are.

For data people, reading diffs fluently is a paying skill: before each commit you see precisely which data transformation just changed - dropna() versus dropna(subset=...) is a difference of thousands of rows in the output.

4. git log - the project history

git log lists the commits, newest first:

git log

Output:

commit 9c4d7e2f1a8b3c5d7e9f0a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d (HEAD -> main)
Author: Duong Do <duong@example.com>
Date:   Mon Aug 3 09:15:22 2026 +0700

    fix dropna to only drop missing revenue

commit 3f2a8b1c9d0e2f4a6b8c0d2e4f6a8b0c2d4e6f8a
Author: Duong Do <duong@example.com>
Date:   Sun Aug 2 16:40:05 2026 +0700

    add revenue cleaning step

Each commit has a hash (a 40-character string - the first 7 characters are usually enough to refer to it), an author, a timestamp and a message. (HEAD -> main) marks where you are standing.

The full form takes space, so day to day you will use three variants:

git log --oneline

Output:

9c4d7e2 (HEAD -> main) fix dropna to only drop missing revenue
3f2a8b1 add revenue cleaning step
a1b2c3d add sales analysis notebook
e5f6a7b initial commit

One line per commit - the bird's-eye view of the whole project. It is also where sloppy messages get exposed: a column full of update and fix makes --oneline useless (lesson 4 of this module).

git log --stat -1

Output:

commit 9c4d7e2f1a8b3c5d7e9f0a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d (HEAD -> main)
Author: Duong Do <duong@example.com>
Date:   Mon Aug 3 09:15:22 2026 +0700

    fix dropna to only drop missing revenue

 src/clean.py | 2 +-
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)

--stat adds a summary of which files changed by how many lines (-1 limits it to one commit). And git log -p prints the full diff of every commit - the definitive answer to "what did this commit really do" when the message cannot be trusted.

Command reference

+-------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|      Command      |                               What it does                               |
+-------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| git status        | The three state compartments: untracked / modified but unstaged / staged |
| git diff          | Edits not yet git add-ed (working directory vs staging)                  |
| git diff --staged | Edits about to be committed (staging vs last commit)                     |
| git diff <file>   | Restrict the diff to one file                                            |
| git log           | Full commit history, newest first                                        |
| git log --oneline | One line per commit - the quick project overview                         |
| git log --stat    | Adds which files changed by how many lines                               |
| git log -p        | Adds the full diff of every commit                                       |
+-------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Key points

  • git status before every decision. It is cheap, changes nothing, and prints the escape hatch for each situation right in its output. Committing blind - no status, no diff - is the fastest way to get junk into history.
  • An empty git diff does not mean lost edits. Edits that were git add-ed moved into git diff --staged territory. The two commands look into two different gaps - remember the three-zone diagram.
  • git diff --staged right before committing. The final check before writing history - it catches hardcoded numbers, debug prints, machine-specific paths.
  • Sloppy messages make git log --oneline useless. History is a reading tool, not a dumping ground; how to write honest messages is lesson 4.

Practice on your machine

Open a terminal and enter the practice repo sales-analysis you built in module 1 (for example cd ~/git-practice/sales-analysis; if you do not have it, quickly git init a new repo and commit one or two files), then create all three states with your own hands and read them.

  1. Confirm a clean starting point:
git status

You must see nothing to commit, working tree clean. If not, commit whatever is in progress before moving on.

  1. Create all three states at once - edit one file and leave it, edit another and stage it, and add a brand-new file:
echo "## Notes" >> README.md
echo "# weekly revenue chart" >> analysis.ipynb
git add analysis.ipynb
mkdir -p src
echo "import pandas as pd" > src/clean.py
git status

You must see exactly three compartments: analysis.ipynb under Changes to be committed, README.md under Changes not staged for commit, and src/ under Untracked files.

  1. Compare the two diff commands looking into two different gaps:
git diff
git diff --staged

git diff shows only the README.md edit (not yet added); git diff --staged shows only the analysis.ipynb edit (already added). Nothing is lost - each command covers one gap.

  1. Gather everything, commit, then read the history back:
git add .
git commit -m "add clean script and notes"
git log --oneline
git log --stat -1

Your new commit must sit on the first line of --oneline, and --stat -1 must list exactly the 3 files you changed.

Self-check:

  • git status in step 2 shows exactly three compartments, each file in the right one as described.
  • git diff and git diff --staged show two DIFFERENT contents, with no file appearing in both.
  • git log --oneline has your new commit on top, marked (HEAD -> main).
  • The final git status reports working tree clean.

lessons.title: Teaching Git what to ignore .gitignore
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 9: Teaching Git what to ignore .gitignore

theory.contentHtml:
Data projects generate junk faster than any other kind: data files hundreds of MB in size, notebook checkpoints, __pycache__, output folders you can regenerate at any time - and most dangerous of all, the .env file holding your database password. .gitignore is the fence that keeps all of it out of history forever, and it costs exactly one text file.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Why data repos fill up with junk
  2. Pattern syntax
  3. A .gitignore for data projects
  4. .gitignore cannot save an already-tracked file
  5. Why is this file ignored?
  6. Command reference
  7. Key points
  8. Practice on your machine

1. Why data repos fill up with junk

Without a .gitignore, after a week of work the git status of sales-analysis/ looks like this:

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        .DS_Store
        .env
        .ipynb_checkpoints/
        data/raw/sales_2026.csv
        outputs/revenue_chart.png
        src/__pycache__/

Each line is its own kind of trouble:

  • Large data files (data/raw/sales_2026.csv) - Git keeps history forever: commit a 500MB file and delete it later, and the repo still weighs 500MB permanently, downloaded by everyone who clones. Raw data belongs somewhere else (a shared drive, S3, a database) - Git manages the code that produces the data, not the data.
  • Secrets (.env) - commit a password once and it lives in history even after the file is deleted. Push it to GitHub and it should be considered leaked.
  • Machine-generated files (__pycache__/, .ipynb_checkpoints/, outputs/) - regenerable from code; their diffs are pure noise.
  • OS junk (.DS_Store) - macOS drops it into every folder; nobody needs it.

Worse still: this pile of untracked files buries the signal. A new data file that should be tracked drowns among two dozen lines of junk, and sooner or later someone runs git add . and sweeps everything into a single commit.

2. Pattern syntax

.gitignore is a text file at the repo root, one pattern per line:

# exact file name - matches at any depth
.DS_Store

# a directory - the trailing slash matters
outputs/

# every file with this extension
*.parquet

# negation: re-include one file that a pattern above ignored
*.csv
!data/sample.csv

Four forms cover 95% of the time:

  • A bare file name (.DS_Store) - matches a file with that name at any directory depth.
  • A directory name with a trailing / (outputs/) - ignores the whole directory and everything inside. It usually works without the slash too, but the slash states the intent: this is a directory.
  • The *.ext wildcard (*.parquet) - every file with that extension, at any depth.
  • Negation with ! (!data/sample.csv) - pulls one file back out of a pattern above it. Exactly the data-project move: ignore every CSV but keep one small sample file of a few dozen rows so anyone who clones can still run the notebook. One trap to know: ! cannot rescue a file inside a directory that is ignored wholesale - once data/raw/ is ignored, !data/raw/sample.csv has no effect.

Lines starting with # are comments. Order matters for !: the negation must come after the pattern it pulls back from.

3. A .gitignore for data projects

A starter set that works for most Python analysis projects:

# large data files do not belong in git
data/raw/
*.parquet
*.csv

# keep one small sample so the notebook runs after clone
!data/sample.csv

# secrets - never in history
.env

# python machinery
__pycache__/
.ipynb_checkpoints/

# regenerable outputs
outputs/

# OS junk
.DS_Store

Once the file exists, git status shrinks instantly:

On branch main
Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        .gitignore

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)

All the junk vanishes from view, leaving only the .gitignore file itself. And that file must be committed: it is part of the project, so the whole team gets the protection, not just your machine:

git add .gitignore
git commit -m "add gitignore for data project"

4. .gitignore cannot save an already-tracked file

The single most misunderstood thing about .gitignore: it only affects untracked files. Once a file is under Git's management, no pattern will help - Git keeps tracking it and git status keeps reporting modified.

The classic situation: you accidentally ran git add data/sales.csv last week, and only now added *.csv to .gitignore - yet the file still shows up in status. The way out is to tell Git to stop tracking while keeping the file on disk:

git rm --cached data/sales.csv

Output:

rm 'data/sales.csv'

Check with git status:

On branch main
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
        deleted:    data/sales.csv

The deleted line only means removed from tracking - the file is still sitting on disk untouched (unlike git rm without --cached, which really deletes it). Commit and it is done:

git commit -m "stop tracking raw sales data"

From now on the *.csv pattern finally applies: the file is no longer tracked, becomes untracked, and is ignored as intended. One thing to understand clearly: the old versions of the file still live in the earlier commits - git rm --cached blocks the future, it does not scrub the past. For a big data file that is acceptable; for a secret that was committed, treat it as leaked and rotate the password, rather than trying to erase history.

5. Why is this file ignored?

A long-lived repo accumulates patterns, and one day you drop in a file only to have git add report it as ignored for no obvious reason. git check-ignore -v names the culprit:

git check-ignore -v data/raw/sales_2026.csv

Output:

.gitignore:2:data/raw/  data/raw/sales_2026.csv

Read it as: this file is ignored by the pattern data/raw/ found on line 2 of the .gitignore file. No more scanning patterns by eye. If the command prints nothing, no pattern is blocking the file - the problem is elsewhere.

Command reference

+----------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|           Command          |                                       What it does                                       |
+----------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| .DS_Store (bare name)      | Ignore a file with that name at any directory depth                                      |
| outputs/                   | Ignore the whole directory and everything inside                                         |
| *.parquet                  | Ignore every file by extension                                                           |
| !data/sample.csv           | Pull one file back out of a pattern above                                                |
| git rm --cached <file>     | Stop tracking but keep the file on disk - the mandatory step for an already-tracked file |
| git check-ignore -v <file> | Show which pattern, in which file on which line, is ignoring this file                   |
+----------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Key points

  • Write the .gitignore when you create the repo, not when the junk appears. Blocking up front is far cheaper than cleaning up later, because tracked files need the extra git rm --cached step.
  • .gitignore has no effect on already-tracked files. This is confusion source number one: you add the pattern and status still says modified. Untrack with git rm --cached, then commit.
  • A committed secret is a leaked secret. git rm --cached does not scrub old commits. The correct response is rotating the password or key, not trying to erase history.
  • Commit the .gitignore file itself. It protects the whole team; it is not a personal machine setting.
  • git check-ignore -v replaces scanning patterns by eye. A mysteriously ignored file - ask Git, do not guess.

Practice on your machine

Still in the practice repo sales-analysis from module 1 (if you do not have it, quickly git init a new repo and commit one or two files), you will create the junk yourself, build the fence, and untrack a file that slipped through.

  1. Create the two most dangerous kinds of junk - a large data file and a secrets file:
mkdir -p data/raw
echo "id,amount" > data/raw/big.csv
echo "DB_PASSWORD=secret123" > .env
git status

Both data/raw/ and .env must appear under Untracked files - waiting for one careless git add ..

  1. Build the fence:
echo "data/raw/" > .gitignore
echo ".env" >> .gitignore
git status

The two junk lines vanish from Untracked files, leaving only the .gitignore file itself.

  1. Ask Git why each file is ignored:
git check-ignore -v data/raw/big.csv
git check-ignore -v .env

Each command prints the pattern plus the line number in .gitignore blocking that file - for example .gitignore:1:data/raw/ data/raw/big.csv.

  1. Commit the fence itself - it is part of the project:
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "add gitignore for data project"
  1. Reproduce the "tracked before ignored" mistake and undo it (-f forces Git to add an ignored file - deliberate, to rebuild the exact situation):
git add -f data/raw/big.csv
git commit -m "accidentally track raw data"
git rm --cached data/raw/big.csv
git commit -m "stop tracking raw data"
git status
ls data/raw

git status reports clean, yet ls data/raw still shows big.csv - the file sits untouched on disk, merely no longer tracked.

Self-check:

  • After step 2, git status no longer shows data/raw/ or .env.
  • git check-ignore -v names the exact pattern and line number for both files.
  • After step 5, big.csv is still on disk but absent from git status.
  • git log --oneline contains the commit pair accidentally track raw data / stop tracking raw data - proof you walked the full mistake-and-fix loop.

theory.contentHtml:
Break a file, stage something you did not mean to commit, mistype a message - sooner or later you will do all of these, and Git has a going-back command for each. But the going-back commands are not equally dangerous: one touches a single uncommitted file, another rewrites history. This lesson orders them by increasing danger, and closes with one rule that picks the right command without memorising much.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. git restore - discard unstaged edits
  2. git restore --staged - pull out of staging
  3. git commit --amend - fix the last commit
  4. git revert - undo with a new commit
  5. git reset --hard - the sharpest knife
  6. The golden rule
  7. Command reference
  8. Key points
  9. Practice on your machine

1. git restore - discard unstaged edits

You have been fiddling with src/clean.py for half an hour, it keeps getting messier, and you want to go back to exactly the version in the last commit:

git restore src/clean.py

The file on disk immediately returns to the last committed version. The command runs silently - verify with git status:

On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean

A warning to read twice: the edits you just discarded are gone for good. They were never committed, so Git holds no copy to rescue them from - no trash bin, no undo. Before any restore, run git diff for one last look at what you are about to throw away.

This is exactly why uncommitted work is the only place in Git where data can truly be lost: everything committed can be recovered somehow; what was never committed cannot.

In older documentation you will meet git checkout -- src/clean.py - the old spelling of the same operation, from before git restore was introduced to untangle checkout's many jobs.

2. git restore --staged - pull out of staging

Ran git add . and swept in a file you did not mean to commit? Pull it back out of staging:

git restore --staged analysis.ipynb

Check with git status:

On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
        modified:   analysis.ipynb

The file drops from the to be committed compartment down to not staged - the edits are intact, they are simply no longer queued for the next commit. This is the gentlest command in the lesson: it does not touch a single byte on disk, it only rearranges what goes into the commit. Do not confuse it with the flagless git restore from section 1 - without --staged you are really discarding edits.

3. git commit --amend - fix the last commit

You commit, then immediately notice a forgotten file or a typo in the message. Do not create a second "fix" commit - repair the last one directly:

git add src/plot.py
git commit --amend --no-edit

--amend folds whatever is staged into the last commit and replaces it with a new one; --no-edit keeps the old message. To fix only the message:

git commit --amend -m "add revenue chart with monthly grouping"

The thing to understand clearly: amend does not edit a commit - it replaces it with a different commit, different hash. Hence exactly one safety condition: that commit has not been pushed. Amending a commit that is already on the remote means your machine's history and the remote's history now tell two different stories about the same spot - teammates who pull will hit confusing conflicts.

4. git revert - undo with a new commit

When the bad commit is already pushed and others may have pulled it, the only safe move is revert:

git revert 3f2a8b1

Output:

[main f3e2d1c] Revert "add dropna for all columns"
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)

revert deletes nothing. It creates a new commit containing the inverse of the named commit - the bad commit stays in history, immediately followed by its fix. History only moves forward, never gets rewritten, so everyone's machine matches as soon as they pull: no conflicts, no surprises.

The price is a history more honest than you might like: anyone reading the log sees both the mistake and the fix. That is not a downside - a Revert "..." line in the log is valuable material for whoever comes next: this spot once went wrong in that particular way.

5. git reset --hard - the sharpest knife

reset --hard drags the current branch to another commit and forces the entire working directory along with it:

git reset --hard HEAD~1

Output:

HEAD is now at 3f2a8b1 add revenue cleaning step

HEAD~1 means "one commit before the current one" - the command above throws the last commit off the branch and wipes every uncommitted edit on disk, without asking. Two losses in one command:

  • The discarded commit can be rescued for a while (Git keeps unreferenced commits around for roughly 30 days, reachable via git reflog) - but that is a salvage operation, not a safety net to rely on.
  • Uncommitted edits are gone for good, exactly as with restore in section 1.

There is a legitimate use: an experimental branch that is yours alone, heading the wrong way, and you want the nearest clean checkpoint - reset --hard is fast and decisive. But the boundary is absolute: never reset --hard past a pushed commit. That is rewriting a stretch of history other people are standing on - every consequence of a misplaced amend, multiplied across the team.

6. The golden rule

This whole lesson compresses into one sentence:

Pushed? revert. Not pushed? amend / reset freely.

Why the boundary sits exactly at push: before pushing, history is your machine's private draft - rewrite it at will, nobody is affected. After pushing, history is a published document - others build on top of it, so you may only append (revert = add one new commit), never rewrite (amend/reset change the hash of something already shared).

As for uncommitted edits: restore is all you need - but always git diff for one last look before throwing them away.

Command reference

+------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|            Command           |                                    What it does                                    |
+------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| git restore <file>           | Discard unstaged edits, back to the last commit - gone for good, unrecoverable     |
| git restore --staged <file>  | Pull out of staging, edits intact - the gentlest command here                      |
| git commit --amend           | Replace the last commit with one folding in the staging area - only while unpushed |
| git commit --amend --no-edit | Same, keeping the message                                                          |
| git revert <hash>            | New commit inverting the named one - safe for shared history                       |
| git reset --hard HEAD~1      | Drop the last commit + wipe all edits on disk - only on unpushed history           |
| git checkout -- <file>       | The old spelling of git restore <file>                                             |
+------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Key points

  • Pushed means revert; unpushed means amend/reset. That one sentence picks the right command for every situation in this lesson. The boundary is the word push: before it history is a private draft, after it a published document.
  • Uncommitted edits are the only thing Git cannot rescue. restore and reset --hard discard them permanently - git diff for one last look before discarding.
  • --staged is the line between gentle and dangerous. git restore --staged merely rearranges staging, nothing is lost; flagless git restore really discards.
  • Amend changes the hash. It replaces the commit rather than editing it in place - which is why it is forbidden on pushed commits.
  • reset --hard is for your own draft history. Great for returning to a clean checkpoint on an experimental branch; past a pushed commit, absolutely not.

Practice on your machine

Still in the practice repo sales-analysis from module 1 (if you do not have it, quickly git init a new repo and commit one or two files), you will cause four classic mistakes yourself and fix each with its own command - everything happens inside the practice repo, so there is nothing to lose.

  1. Break a file, then rescue it with restore - remember to look at git diff before discarding:
echo "BROKEN LINE" >> README.md
git diff
git restore README.md
git status

git diff must show the line +BROKEN LINE; after restore, git status reports working tree clean and the broken line is gone from the file.

  1. Stage by mistake, then pull back out - the edits survive:
echo "temp note" >> README.md
git add README.md
git restore --staged README.md
git status
git restore README.md

After restore --staged, the file drops into the Changes not staged compartment - the edits are still intact on disk. The final restore just cleans up for the next step.

  1. Commit with a mistyped message, then amend:
echo "chart: weekly revenue" >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "wrogn mesage"
git commit --amend -m "add weekly revenue note to readme"
git log --oneline -2

git log must show only ONE commit for this change, carrying the corrected message - the wrogn mesage commit is gone because it was replaced by a different commit with a different hash.

  1. Commit a "wrong" change, then invert it with revert:
echo "WRONG NUMBER: 999" >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "add wrong revenue number"
git revert --no-edit HEAD
git log --oneline -3

The log must contain BOTH the bad commit and the Revert "add wrong revenue number" commit sitting above it; open README.md - the line WRONG NUMBER: 999 is gone even though no commit was deleted.

Self-check:

  • Step 1: the line BROKEN LINE is no longer in the file and git status is clean.
  • Step 2: after restore --staged, the file sits in the not staged compartment - proving only staging was undone, no edits lost.
  • Step 3: git log --oneline no longer contains the message wrogn mesage, and there is no second "fix message" commit.
  • Step 4: history keeps the bad commit plus a revert commit, and the file is free of the bad line - exactly the spirit of "once written, only append, never rewrite".
