theory.contentHtml:
Git histories come in two kinds: the kind that reads like an analysis journal - every step clear, any point recoverable - and the kind that is a string of update, fix, final_v2 saying nothing at all. The difference is not the tool but commit habits. This lesson is that set of habits, tailored for data people.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Atomic commits - one job per commit
  2. Why "update" is a useless message
  3. The shape of an honest message
  4. A commit rhythm for data analysis
  5. Untangling two jobs done at once
  6. Command reference
  7. Key points
  8. Practice on your machine

1. Atomic commits - one job per commit

A good commit is atomic: it contains exactly one complete change - one cleaning step, one chart, one fix. Not for tidiness' sake, but because every Git tool operates on the commit as its unit:

  • Readable: git log --oneline retells the work in order, one step per line.
  • Individually revertible: new chart broke something? git revert exactly that commit; the cleaning step in another commit is untouched. A commit mixing five jobs reverts all five at once.
  • Traceable: when a number in the report shifts unexpectedly, walking atomic commits points to exactly which transformation caused it; walking through a 400-line "changes" commit gets you nowhere.

Atomic does not mean tiny. A cleaning step that touches three files is still one job - the boundary is this: you can describe the commit in one sentence without the word "and". "Fix the cleaning step and add a chart and change the colours" - that is three commits.

2. Why "update" is a useless message

Two histories of the same week of work. The first:

b7c8d9e update
a6b7c8d fix
95a6b7c changes
84950a6 final
7383941 final final

The second:

b7c8d9e add weekly revenue trend chart
a6b7c8d exclude test orders from revenue sum
95a6b7c drop rows with missing revenue
84950a6 load raw sales csv into notebook
7383941 initial commit

Three months later, your boss asks: "Why is Q2 revenue in the August report different from the July version?" With the second history, the line exclude test orders from revenue sum practically is the answer. With the first, you are running git log -p and re-reading every diff - doing archaeology on yourself.

The treacherous part of a sloppy message is that writing it does not hurt at the time: you just finished the work, everything is fresh in your head, "update" feels sufficient. The bill arrives weeks later, once the context has evaporated - and by then it cannot be fixed. A message is written once and read many times, by a reader guaranteed to have forgotten everything: you, three months from now.

3. The shape of an honest message

The Git community's shared template:

  • First line ≤ 50–72 characters, in the imperative: add revenue chart, not added or adding. The test: the first line must fit the sentence "If applied, this commit will …" - "…add revenue chart" reads naturally, "…added revenue chart" does not. The length limit is not cosmetic: git log --oneline and GitHub's UI truncate long lines, and an oversized message is a message read half-cut.
  • The body explains WHY, whenever the reason is not obvious. What changed, the diff already says; what the diff cannot say is why it had to change. Separate it from the first line with one blank line:
drop rows with missing revenue

Revenue is NULL for test orders created by the payment team.
Keeping them inflates the order count by about 3 percent and
skews average order value, so they are removed before any
aggregation happens.

Three months later, when someone wonders "why were these rows dropped?", the answer sits right inside git log - no digging through chat, no asking someone who has left. For a small self-explanatory change, the first line alone is enough; do not pad a body for the sake of it.

A one-line message written straight in the command:

git commit -m "drop rows with missing revenue"

When you need a body, run git commit without -m - Git opens an editor for the multi-line message.

4. A commit rhythm for data analysis

Data analysis has a natural rhythm: load the data → clean → transform → chart → conclude. The best commit rhythm follows exactly those steps - finish a step, re-run and see it is right, commit that step:

git add analysis.ipynb
git commit -m "load raw sales csv into notebook"

git add src/clean.py
git commit -m "drop rows with missing revenue"

git add analysis.ipynb
git commit -m "add weekly revenue trend chart"

Compare with the end-of-day habit of piling everything into one "changes" commit: the same amount of work, but the former gives you checkpoints along the way. The chart wrecked the notebook? Return to the checkpoint right after cleaning; the day is not lost. The "changes" version has only two states: start of day and end of day - all or nothing.

The right moment to commit is when a step is complete and its result was just verified: the notebook re-runs from the top without errors, the sanity-check numbers match. Do not commit half-running code just because "it has been a while" - a commit is a milestone meaning a step is done, not a timer.

5. Untangling two jobs done at once

Real life is not tidy: while adding a chart in analysis.ipynb you fix a cleaning bug in src/clean.py along the way. By the end of the session, two unrelated jobs sit together in the working directory. This is where the staging area - the seemingly redundant buffer from the previous module - answers the question "what is it for": it lets you choose piece by piece what goes into which commit:

git add src/clean.py
git commit -m "fix revenue cleaning to keep zero-value orders"

git add analysis.ipynb
git commit -m "add weekly revenue trend chart"

Verify with git log --oneline:

f3e2d1c (HEAD -> main) add weekly revenue trend chart
9c4d7e2 fix revenue cleaning to keep zero-value orders

Two jobs, two commits, each individually revertible - even though the work itself was tangled. Staging is precisely the untangling tool for after the fact, so tangling while working is fine; a tangled commit is the problem.

When the two jobs are mixed inside the same file, git add -p (patch mode) walks you through the diff hunk by hunk - stage this piece, leave that one for later. Knowing it exists is enough; fluent or not, the closing rule stands: never let two jobs share one commit.

Command reference

+---------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
|          Command          |                           What it does                          |
+---------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
| git commit -m "<message>" | Commit with a one-line message written in the command           |
| git commit                | Opens the editor - for messages that need a body explaining why |
| git add <file>            | Stage file by file - the foundation of splitting commits        |
| git add -p                | Walk the diff hunk by hunk, untangling two jobs inside one file |
| git log --oneline         | Where good and sloppy messages are most exposed                 |
| git show <hash>           | Show one commit's message plus its full diff                    |
+---------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------+

Key points

  • One commit, one job - describable in one sentence without "and". A sentence with "and" is the signal to split; atomicity is what makes individual reverts and step-by-step tracing possible.
  • The message is written for you, three months from now. "update" does not hurt when written, only when read. First line ≤ 50–72 characters, imperative (add, not added), tested against "If applied, this commit will …".
  • The diff says what, the body says why. The business reason - why these rows were dropped, why test orders were excluded - lives only in the message, and it is the most valuable thing when a number gets questioned.
  • Commit by analysis step, not by the clock. Load done → commit, cleaning done → commit, chart done → commit. Every milestone is a verified point of return.
  • Two jobs got tangled? Untangle at add time. git add file by file, or git add -p hunk by hunk within a file. Tangling while working is normal; tangling inside a commit is the problem.

Practice on your machine

Still in the practice repo sales-analysis from module 1 (if you do not have it, quickly git init a new repo and commit one or two files), you will deliberately tangle two jobs inside ONE file and then split them into two honest commits.

  1. Build a report file long enough that the two edits sit far apart:
seq -f "line-%02g" 12 > report.txt
git add report.txt
git commit -m "add report skeleton"
  1. Do two unrelated jobs in the same file: open report.txt in your editor, change the first line line-01 to title: monthly revenue, save; then add a footer with the command:
echo "footer: generated by sales-analysis" >> report.txt
git diff report.txt

The diff must show TWO separate hunks - two distinct @@ sections, one at the top of the file (title), one at the bottom (footer). This is exactly "two jobs tangled inside one file".

  1. Split with patch mode - stage only the title hunk:
git add -p report.txt

Git stops at each hunk and asks Stage this hunk ...? - type y for the title hunk, n for the footer hunk. Verify, then commit the first job:

git diff --staged
git commit -m "set report title to monthly revenue"

git diff --staged must contain only the title hunk - the footer stays outside.

  1. Commit the second job, then read the history back:
git add report.txt
git commit -m "add generated-by footer to report"
git log --oneline -3

Three lines, three jobs: footer → title → skeleton. Each message imperative, one sentence, no "and".

Self-check:

  • git diff in step 2 shows exactly two @@ hunks inside one file.
  • git diff --staged after git add -p contains only the title change, no footer.
  • git log --oneline -3 shows three separate commits with imperative messages (set, add), each describable in one sentence without "and".
  • Ask yourself: if you git revert the footer commit, is the title affected? (No - that is the payoff of atomic commits.)

questions.prompt: You edit src/clean.py, run git add src/clean.py, then type git diff - and see nothing at all. What happened?

options.label: A
options.text: The edits are lost and must be recovered from the last commit

options.label: B
options.text: The edits moved into staging; plain git diff only compares the working directory with staging - use git diff --staged to see them

options.label: C
options.text: git diff only works before git add; the only option now is to commit and inspect with git show

options.label: D
options.text: .py files need a special flag before git diff will display them

questions.explanation: Plain git diff compares the working directory with the staging area - it only shows edits NOT yet git add-ed. After the add, the edits sit in the gap between staging and the last commit, which is git diff --staged territory; run that and they reappear in full. Nothing is lost, so (a) is wrong - and that misunderstanding is dangerous, because someone might rush to restore in order to "rescue" something that was never gone. (c) is doubly wrong: git diff --staged works immediately with no commit needed, and running order does not disable the command. (d) is made up - diff does not discriminate by file type.

questions.prompt: You add the line *.csv to .gitignore, but git status still reports modified: data/sales.csv. Why, and what is the fix?

options.label: A
options.text: The pattern syntax is wrong - it must be data/*.csv to match files in subdirectories

options.label: B
options.text: You must run git restore data/sales.csv so Git re-reads the .gitignore

options.label: C
options.text: .gitignore only affects untracked files; data/sales.csv was already tracked, so run git rm --cached data/sales.csv and commit

options.label: D
options.text: CSV files count as data, which Git always tracks and can never ignore

questions.explanation: This is the single most misunderstood thing about .gitignore: it only keeps untracked files from being added - a file already under Git's management stays tracked no matter what patterns match it. The way out is git rm --cached data/sales.csv - stop tracking while keeping the file on disk - followed by a commit; the file then becomes untracked and the pattern finally applies. (a) is wrong because *.csv matches at every directory depth - syntax is not the problem. (b) is wrong: git restore is the discard-edits command, has nothing to do with re-reading .gitignore, and running it would actually destroy your current edits. (d) is made up - Git does not discriminate by file type.

questions.prompt: Commit a1b2c3d broke the dashboard numbers. It is ALREADY pushed to the remote and teammates have most likely pulled it. What is the correct fix?

options.label: A
options.text: git reset --hard a1b2c3d~1 and force-push to erase the bad commit entirely

options.label: B
options.text: git commit --amend to edit the bad commit's content directly

options.label: C
options.text: git restore . to return every file to its state before the bad commit

options.label: D
options.text: git revert a1b2c3d - create a new commit inverting the bad one, then push normally

questions.explanation: The golden rule: pushed means revert. git revert creates a NEW commit containing the inverse - history only moves forward instead of being rewritten, so teammates' machines match as soon as they pull, with no conflicts. (a) rewrites shared history: after the force-push, every machine that pulled the old commit is out of sync with the remote, and the whole team lands in messy conflicts. (b) is wrong twice: --amend can only touch the LAST commit (not necessarily a1b2c3d), and by nature it replaces the commit with a different hash - also rewriting pushed history. (c) is the wrong tool: git restore operates on uncommitted edits in the working directory; it cannot invert a commit that is already part of history.

questions.prompt: You have been fiddling with analysis.ipynb for a while, the results keep getting worse, and nothing was ever git add-ed. You want to throw away all the edits and return to the last committed version. Which command, and what must you know before typing it?

options.label: A
options.text: git restore --staged analysis.ipynb - safe because the edits are preserved

options.label: B
options.text: git restore analysis.ipynb - knowing that uncommitted edits, once discarded, are gone for good with no way back

options.label: C
options.text: git revert analysis.ipynb - create an inverse commit for this file

options.label: D
options.text: git reset --hard HEAD~1 - going back one full commit is the most thorough option

questions.explanation: git restore <file> returns the working-directory file to its last committed version - exactly the need here. The thing you must understand: these edits were NEVER committed, so Git holds no copy to rescue them from - discarding is permanent, which is why you git diff for one last look before typing. (a) does not do the job: --staged only pulls a file out of staging (and nothing is staged here anyway); the edits on disk remain untouched. (c) is wrong in both syntax and concept: revert takes a COMMIT hash, not a file name, and it inverts a commit in history rather than cleaning the working directory. (d) is overkill aimed at the wrong target: reset --hard HEAD~1 also throws away the last commit - the very version you are trying to return TO - along with every other file's uncommitted edits.

questions.prompt: At the end of a session, your working directory holds two unrelated jobs: a cleaning bug fix in src/clean.py and a new chart in analysis.ipynb. What is the best way to commit?

options.label: A
options.text: git add . and commit the lot with the message update - quick now, split it tomorrow

options.label: B
options.text: Commit both together with a very long message listing both jobs - a detailed enough message makes mixing fine

options.label: C
options.text: git add src/clean.py → commit fix revenue cleaning to keep zero-value orders, then git add analysis.ipynb → commit add weekly revenue trend chart

options.label: D
options.text: Commit only the chart; save the fix to batch with other fixes into one fixes commit later

questions.explanation: The staging area exists precisely for this situation: git add file by file splits two tangled jobs into two atomic commits - each a complete story, individually revertible, individually traceable. (a) creates a mixed commit with a useless message; "split it tomorrow" is a fantasy - untangling an already-pushed commit into clean pieces is a job almost nobody comes back to do. (b) misses the point: a long message cannot fix the fact that git revert works at COMMIT granularity - removing just the chart would drag the bug fix out with it. (d) is bad in the other direction: a fix that is done and verified belongs in history now; hoarding it to batch into a fixes commit later creates exactly the mixed commit you are trying to avoid.

You open the repo and git status prints:


On branch main
Changes to be committed:

        modified:   src/clean.py

Changes not staged for commit:

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        data/sales.csv


If you type git commit -m "..." right now (without adding anything else), what happens?

options.label: A
options.text: All three files go into the commit - commit always snapshots the whole working directory

options.label: B
options.text: Only the edits to src/clean.py are committed; analysis.ipynb keeps its edits on disk but outside the commit, and data/sales.csv stays untracked

options.label: C
options.text: Both modified files go into the commit, while data/sales.csv is left out because it is untracked

options.label: D
options.text: Git refuses to commit while untracked files remain in the repo

questions.explanation: A commit records only what sits in STAGING - exactly the *Changes to be committed* compartment, here src/clean.py. analysis.ipynb is tracked and has edits, but they were never git add-ed, so they stay in the working directory, outside the commit. data/sales.csv was never tracked at all, so it is even further from this commit. (a) confuses commit with "snapshotting the whole scene" - staging is precisely the selection step in between; to get that behaviour you would have to run git add . deliberately first. (c) is wrong because the two modified files are NOT equals: one is staged, one is not - status putting them in two different compartments is exactly how it tells you that. (d) is made up - untracked files never block a commit; Git merely reminds you that they exist.

questions.prompt:
You just edited src/clean.py and want to commit the change. Two check commands show:


$ git diff --staged

$ git diff
diff --git a/src/clean.py b/src/clean.py
index 3f2a8b1..9c4d7e2 100644
--- a/src/clean.py
+++ b/src/clean.py
@@ -4,5 +4,5 @@ import pandas as pd

 def load_sales(path):
     df = pd.read_csv(path)
-    df = df.dropna()
+    df = df.dropna(subset=["revenue"])
     return df


Why is git diff --staged empty, and what is the next step to get this change committed?

options.label: A
options.text: The edits are already staged; git diff --staged is empty only because the output is cached - just type git commit

options.label: B
options.text: The edits were never git add-ed - --staged compares staging with the last commit, and staging currently matches it, hence empty; run git add src/clean.py, then commit

options.label: C
options.text: An empty git diff --staged means the file is not tracked by Git yet - git add is needed to track it for the first time

options.label: D
options.text: Just type git commit - commit automatically gathers every edit in the working directory, so no add is needed

questions.explanation: git diff --staged compares STAGING with the last commit - empty means nothing has been queued for the next commit. git diff (no arguments) compares the working directory with staging - showing content means the edits sit outside staging, i.e. not yet git add-ed. The correct path: git add src/clean.py, re-check with git diff --staged (it will now show the dropna hunk), then commit. (a) invents a mechanism - Git does not cache diff output; empty is the true state of staging. (c) is wrong: untracked files never appear in git diff at all, and the output here has the index, a/, b/ lines - proof the file is tracked and being compared against its old version. (d) is wrong: bare git commit records only what is in staging, and with staging empty Git reports no changes added to commit; sweeping the working directory automatically is the -a flag, and relying on it skips the git diff --staged review before writing history.

lessons.title: Branches experiment without fear
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 15: Branches experiment without fear

theory.contentHtml:
Your notebook works: it reads the data, cleans it, trains a model you can live with. Now you want to try a new feature-engineering idea - but if you try it directly on the working code and it breaks, how do you get back? Branches are Git's answer to exactly that question: a place to experiment freely, throw it away if it fails, keep it if it works, and the working version is never touched.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. A familiar situation: backup by copying files
  2. A branch is a pointer to a commit
  3. Creating a branch and switching back and forth
  4. HEAD: where you are standing
  5. Switching branches rewrites files on disk
  6. Name branches after the work
  7. Command reference
  8. Key points
  9. Practice on your machine

1. A familiar situation: backup by copying files

The traditional way data people experiment looks like this:

analysis.ipynb
analysis_v2.ipynb
analysis_v2_final.ipynb
analysis_v2_final_FIXED.ipynb

Three weeks later, nobody remembers which one works, which one holds the half-finished experiment, and the only way to see how two of them differ is to open both and compare by eye. Copying the whole project folder is even worse: a few GB of data duplicated just to change a few dozen lines of code.

A branch solves exactly that worry - "I want to try something without breaking the working version" - but copies nothing.

2. A branch is a pointer to a commit

You already know Git history is a chain of commits. The surprise: a branch is just a pointer to one commit - inside .git, it is a file of a few dozen bytes containing exactly the hash of the commit it points at. Nothing more.

The repo currently has this history:

git log --oneline

Output:

9f3e2a1 (HEAD -> main) train baseline model
4c8b7d2 add mean encoding features
1a5f9c3 initial notebook

main is just a branch too - a pointer currently at 9f3e2a1. List the branches you have:

git branch

Output:

* main

Because a branch is only a pointer, creating one is virtually free: a repo with 2 GB of data or 2 KB of code, it makes no difference - Git just writes one tiny file. No folder is copied. This is why Git users create a branch for every little experiment without a second thought - a very different instinct from "copy the folder to be safe".

3. Creating a branch and switching back and forth

Create a branch for the log-transform experiment, and switch onto it, in one command:

git switch -c try-log-transform

Output:

Switched to a new branch 'try-log-transform'

The -c flag (create) does two things: creates the branch at the current commit, then moves you onto it. (Older material often uses git checkout -b try-log-transform - same effect; git switch is the newer command split out for clarity, and this lesson uses it throughout.)

git branch

Output:

  main
* try-log-transform

The * marks the branch you are standing on. Now edit freely - add the log transform to src/features.py and commit:

git add src/features.py
git commit -m "try log transform on skewed columns"

Output:

[try-log-transform 7e4d1b8] try log transform on skewed columns
 1 file changed, 12 insertions(+)

Look at the whole picture with --all (without it, git log shows only the history of the branch you are on):

git log --oneline --all

Output:

7e4d1b8 (HEAD -> try-log-transform) try log transform on skewed columns
9f3e2a1 (main) train baseline model
4c8b7d2 add mean encoding features
1a5f9c3 initial notebook

Notice the most important thing: main has not moved - it still sits at 9f3e2a1. The new commit only pushed the try-log-transform pointer forward:

1a5f9c3 --- 4c8b7d2 --- 9f3e2a1 --- 7e4d1b8
                           ^           ^
                          main   try-log-transform

You can commit ten times on this branch and main will not budge. Experiment failed? Switch back to main, delete the branch, and it is as if nothing happened.

4. HEAD: where you are standing

The output above shows HEAD -> try-log-transform. HEAD is the answer to "where am I standing" - it points at the current branch, and that branch points at a commit. See for yourself:

cat .git/HEAD

Output:

ref: refs/heads/try-log-transform

The chain of delegation is: HEAD → branch → commit. When you commit, Git creates the new commit and then slides the branch HEAD points at up to it. Since HEAD points at try-log-transform, only that pointer moves - main is not involved. That is the entire mechanism behind "commits on a branch never touch main".

5. Switching branches rewrites files on disk

This is the biggest surprise for newcomers. Switch back to main:

git switch main

Output:

Switched to branch 'main'

Open src/features.py right now: the 12 lines of log transform are gone. Not truly gone - they sit safely in commit 7e4d1b8 on the other branch - but Git has rewritten the file on disk to match the commit main points at. Switching branches does not just change some abstract "context": real file contents, on the real disk, change. An editor with the file open will see its contents jump; so will a notebook open in Jupyter - reload after switching branches.

And because switching touches files, Git refuses to switch if you have uncommitted changes that would be overwritten:

error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by checkout:
	src/features.py
Please commit your changes or stash them before you switch branches.
Aborting

When you see this, just commit first and then switch - commits on an experiment branch are free, and you know from the earlier lesson that small commits are nothing to regret.

6. Name branches after the work

A branch name is something you read back three weeks later, with all context forgotten. Name it after the work it is for:

try-log-transform
fix-nulls-in-loader
add-holiday-features

not after your mood:

test
new
final2

The simple rule: the name alone should answer "what was this branch born to do" without opening the code. When git branch lists eight names like test2, even you will not dare delete any of them.

Command reference

+-------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
|         Command         |                            What it does                           |
+-------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| git branch              | Lists local branches, * marks the one you are on                  |
| git switch -c <name>    | Creates a branch at the current commit and switches onto it       |
| git switch <name>       | Switches to an existing branch - files on disk change accordingly |
| git checkout -b <name>  | The old way, same effect as git switch -c                         |
| git log --oneline --all | Shows the history of every branch, with each pointer's position   |
| cat .git/HEAD           | Shows which branch HEAD points at                                 |
+-------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------+

Key points

A branch is a pointer, not a copy. Creating one writes a single file of a few dozen bytes, so make a branch for every experiment - there is nothing to save on.

Commits on a branch never touch main. Only the branch HEAD points at moves. If the experiment fails, switch back to main and everything is intact.

Switching branches rewrites real files on disk. Not an illusion - open a file and its contents are different. Editors and Jupyter need a reload after switching.

A branch name must state the work. try-log-transform reads itself; three weeks later even you will give up on final2.

Practice on your machine

Now walk the full life cycle of an experiment branch yourself, in the practice repo ~/git-practice/sales-analysis - if you do not have it yet, create one quickly: mkdir -p ~/git-practice/sales-analysis && cd ~/git-practice/sales-analysis && git init && echo "date,amount" > sales.csv && git add . && git commit -m "init practice repo".

  1. Enter the practice repo and check the starting point:
cd ~/git-practice/sales-analysis
git status
git log --oneline

You should see working tree clean and at least one commit.

  1. Create the experiment branch and switch onto it:
git switch -c try-log-transform
git branch

You should see Switched to a new branch 'try-log-transform', and in the branch list the * sits in front of try-log-transform.

  1. Edit a file and commit right on the branch:
echo "log_transform = True" >> analysis.txt
git add analysis.txt
git commit -m "try log transform"

The first output line must open with [try-log-transform ...] - the commit lands on the experiment branch, not main.

  1. Look at the whole picture of both branches:
git log --oneline --all

The newest commit must carry (HEAD -> try-log-transform), while (main) sits at an older commit - main has not budged.

  1. Switch back to main and look at the file on disk:
git switch main
cat analysis.txt

The line log_transform = True must be gone - if the file was only born in step 3, cat even reports No such file or directory: on main, the other branch's content does not exist.

  1. Switch back to the branch and confirm the content returns:
git switch try-log-transform
cat analysis.txt

The line log_transform = True is back - switching branches rewrites real files on disk, exactly as the lesson said.

Self-check:

  • git branch lists both branches and the * sits on the branch you are standing on.
  • git log --oneline --all shows main and try-log-transform pointing at two different commits.
  • The contents of analysis.txt change with every git switch - and you can explain why nothing is lost.

lessons.title: Merging bringing experiments home
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 16: Merging bringing experiments home

theory.contentHtml:
The log-transform experiment worked: the model really did improve. Now the commits sitting on try-log-transform need to come home to main - the branch that holds the official version. That operation is a merge, and it is far cheaper than its scary reputation: most merges, Git finishes by itself in a second.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Stand on the receiving branch
  2. Fast-forward: just sliding the pointer
  3. Merge commit: when both sides have moved
  4. Reading the commit graph
  5. Deleting branches after the merge
  6. Command reference
  7. Key points
  8. Practice on your machine

1. Stand on the receiving branch

git merge pulls changes into the branch you are standing on. If main is to receive the results, you must stand on main and name the other branch:

git switch main
git merge try-log-transform

Getting the direction backwards is the most common beginner mistake: standing on try-log-transform and typing git merge main. Nothing breaks, but the result is the opposite of what you wanted - main stays exactly as it was, while your experiment branch gets main mixed into it. Before any merge, ask one question: "which branch receives?" - then stand there.

2. Fast-forward: just sliding the pointer

The situation right now: since the branch was created, main has had no new commits. The two branches still lie on one straight line:

--- 9f3e2a1 --- 7e4d1b8
       ^           ^
      main   try-log-transform

Merging this shape requires no "blending" at all - the history of try-log-transform already contains the entire history of main, so Git simply slides the main pointer forward:

git merge try-log-transform

Output:

Updating 9f3e2a1..7e4d1b8
Fast-forward
 src/features.py | 12 ++++++++++++
 1 file changed, 12 insertions(+)

Fast-forward means exactly that: wind the pointer forward. No new commit is created - after the command, both labels point at the same commit:

--- 9f3e2a1 --- 7e4d1b8
                   ^
       main, try-log-transform

3. Merge commit: when both sides have moved

The next experiment: you branch off try-scaling to try feature scaling, but this time, while you work on the branch, main also gains a commit (you quickly fixed a date-parsing bug). History has genuinely forked:

             5d9c3e7  fix date parsing (main)
            /
--- 7e4d1b8
            \
             8b1a4f6  scale features (try-scaling)

This time sliding a pointer is no longer possible - each side has commits the other lacks. Git must create a merge commit: a special commit with two parents, gathering the changes of both lines into one point:

git switch main
git merge try-scaling

Git opens your editor with a prepared message Merge branch 'try-scaling' - save and close, done:

Merge made by the 'ort' strategy.
 src/features.py | 8 ++++++++
 1 file changed, 8 insertions(+)

(ort is the name of Git's current default merge strategy - nothing you need to care about.) The two sides changed different places, so Git blended them by itself. The case where both sides change the same line - next lesson.

4. Reading the commit graph

After a merge commit, history is no longer a straight line. The command worth memorising:

git log --oneline --graph --all

Output:

*   c2f8e5d (HEAD -> main) Merge branch 'try-scaling'
|\
| * 8b1a4f6 (try-scaling) scale features before training
* | 5d9c3e7 fix date parsing in loader
|/
* 7e4d1b8 try log transform on skewed columns
* 9f3e2a1 train baseline model
* 4c8b7d2 add mean encoding features
* 1a5f9c3 initial notebook

How to read it: each * is a commit, the vertical lines are branches running in parallel. The graph puts the newest commit on top, so the two forking symbols read backwards against time: |\ right under the merge commit is where the two branches joined back, and |/ further down is where history split off the common commit 7e4d1b8. The top commit is the merge commit - it sits where two lines converge into one. From this graph you can retell the whole story: when the branch split, what each side did, where they merged.

5. Deleting branches after the merge

The results are in main; the try-scaling label has no job left. Clean it up:

git branch -d try-scaling

Output:

Deleted branch try-scaling (was 8b1a4f6).

Recall the previous lesson: a branch is only a pointer. Deleting a branch deletes the label, not the commits - 8b1a4f6 still sits in main's history, and git log still shows it. That is why deleting a merged branch is perfectly safe.

The lowercase -d also protects you: if the branch is not merged yet, it refuses:

git branch -d try-dropout

Output:

error: the branch 'try-dropout' is not fully merged
hint: If you are sure you want to delete it, run 'git branch -D try-dropout'

-D (uppercase) is the forced version: delete regardless. Use it only when you are certain you want to discard that experiment - once the label is gone, the unmerged commits have no name pointing at them; recoverable, but hard to find. Good habit: -d first, and only consider -D when Git objects.

Command reference

+---------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------+
|             Command             |                      What it does                      |
+---------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------+
| git merge <branch>              | Merges that branch into the branch you are standing on |
| git log --oneline --graph --all | Draws the commit graph of every branch                 |
| git branch -d <branch>          | Deletes a merged branch - refuses if not merged        |
| git branch -D <branch>          | Force-deletes a branch even if unmerged                |
| git branch --merged             | Lists branches fully merged into the current branch    |
+---------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------+

Key points

Merge pulls into the branch you are standing on. Before typing the command, ask "which branch receives?" and git switch there. Standing on the wrong side mixes main backwards into your experiment branch.

A fast-forward creates no commit; a merge commit has two parents. main has not moved → slide the pointer; both sides have moved → one commit joins the two lines. The first line of the output tells you which one just happened.

Deleting a branch deletes a label, not commits. For a merged branch, -d is perfectly safe. -D is the one that deserves a second thought.

Practice on your machine

Create both kinds of merge yourself - a fast-forward, then a merge commit - in the practice repo ~/git-practice/sales-analysis; if you do not have it yet, create one quickly: mkdir -p ~/git-practice/sales-analysis && cd ~/git-practice/sales-analysis && git init && echo "date,amount" > sales.csv && git add . && git commit -m "init practice repo".

  1. Set up the fast-forward situation: one branch moves, main stands still:
cd ~/git-practice/sales-analysis
git switch main
git switch -c add-notes
echo "note: check outliers" >> notes.txt
git add notes.txt
git commit -m "add analysis notes"

The new commit sits on add-notes; since the branch split off, main has not taken a single step.

  1. Stand on the receiving branch and merge:
git switch main
git merge add-notes

The output must contain Fast-forward - Git only slides the pointer, creating no new commit.

  1. Confirm both labels point at the same commit:
git log --oneline

The top line must carry (HEAD -> main, add-notes) - two names, one commit.

  1. Set up the both-sides-moved situation: commit on a new branch, then commit again on main:
git switch -c add-readme
echo "sales analysis practice repo" >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "add readme"
git switch main
echo "note: fix date parsing" >> notes.txt
git add notes.txt
git commit -m "add date parsing note"

Now each side has a commit the other lacks - sliding a pointer is no longer possible.

  1. Merge again - this time it produces a merge commit:
git merge add-readme -m "Merge branch 'add-readme'"

The output must contain Merge made by the 'ort' strategy. (the -m flag just keeps Git from opening an editor).

  1. Read the graph:
git log --oneline --graph --all

At the top is the two-parent merge commit; following the vertical lines you must see |\ right under it (where the branches join) and |/ further down (where history split off the common commit).

  1. Clean up the merged branches:
git branch -d add-notes
git branch -d add-readme
git branch

Two Deleted branch ... lines, and the branch list shrinks - deleting merged labels loses no commits.

Self-check:

  • The first merge prints Fast-forward, the second prints Merge made by the 'ort' strategy. - you can say why the two results differ.
  • git log --oneline --graph --all draws exactly one split and one join.
  • git branch -d deletes both branches without complaint - because the results already sit fully in main.

lessons.title: Conflicts when two changes collide
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 19: Conflicts when two changes collide

theory.contentHtml:
Sooner or later it happens: you type git merge, and instead of a peaceful Merge made by... line, Git stops halfway with CONFLICT in capital letters. Newcomers who see that word usually think they have just broken the repo. Nothing is broken - this lesson teaches you to read what Git is saying, and to sort it out in minutes.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. A conflict is not an error
  2. Reproducing a conflict
  3. Reading the conflict markers
  4. Resolving by hand
  5. Backing out: git merge --abort
  6. The data person's special pain: notebooks
  7. Command reference
  8. Key points
  9. Practice on your machine

1. A conflict is not an error

When two branches change different places - even inside the same file - Git blends them by itself, as you saw last lesson. A conflict only happens when two branches change the same line in two different ways. At that point, which version to keep is a business decision, not an algorithmic one: whether the outlier threshold should be 5 or 20 can only be answered by someone who understands the data.

So read CONFLICT for what it really means: Git refuses to guess. It stops, shows you exactly where the two changes collide, and waits for your ruling. That is the correct behaviour - a tool that silently picked for you would be the scary one.

2. Reproducing a conflict

Create a conflict on purpose and look at it up close. The file src/clean.py currently has the line THRESHOLD = 10. On a new branch, lower the threshold to 5:

git switch -c fix-threshold
# edit src/clean.py: THRESHOLD = 5
git commit -am "lower outlier threshold to 5"

Back on main - having forgotten about the other branch - raise that same line to 20:

git switch main
# edit src/clean.py: THRESHOLD = 20
git commit -am "raise outlier threshold to 20"

The two branches now change the same line in two ways. Try to merge:

git merge fix-threshold

Output:

Auto-merging src/clean.py
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/clean.py
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

Git stops and waits. git status tells you where you stand:

git status

Output:

On branch main
You have unmerged paths.
  (fix conflicts and run "git commit")
  (use "git merge --abort" to abort the merge)

Unmerged paths:
  (use "git add <file>..." to mark resolution)
	both modified:   src/clean.py

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")

git status even prints both exits for you: finish resolving then git commit, or retreat with git merge --abort.

3. Reading the conflict markers

Open src/clean.py - Git has inserted marker lines at exactly the disputed spot:

import pandas as pd

<<<<<<< HEAD
THRESHOLD = 20
=======
THRESHOLD = 5
>>>>>>> fix-threshold

def remove_outliers(df):
    return df[df["value"] < THRESHOLD]

Reading each marker line:

  • <<<<<<< HEAD opens the version from the branch you are standing on (HEAD - here, main): THRESHOLD = 20.
  • ======= is the divider between the two versions.
  • >>>>>>> fix-threshold closes the version from the branch being merged in: THRESHOLD = 5.

Everything else in the file - the import, the remove_outliers function - Git has already merged cleanly. Only the section between the markers awaits your ruling.

4. Resolving by hand

"Resolving" means: edit the file into its final, correct version. You have full authority - keep main's version, keep fix-threshold's, keep both (when they are two independent lines), or write something new that matches neither. Git has no opinion; right and wrong are yours to decide.

Here you decide 20 is the correct threshold. Edit the file into:

import pandas as pd

THRESHOLD = 20

def remove_outliers(df):
    return df[df["value"] < THRESHOLD]

Two things are mandatory: choose the final version, and delete all three marker lines. A leftover marker means <<<<<<< sitting in the middle of Python code - the next run blows up with a SyntaxError on that exact line. (This is the most common leave-behind mistake after resolving a conflict.)

Then tell Git this file is done:

git add src/clean.py
git commit

Here git add means "I have resolved this file". git commit opens your editor with the prepared message Merge branch 'fix-threshold' - save, close:

[main 3e7f2c9] Merge branch 'fix-threshold'

The merge is complete, and history gains a merge commit just like last lesson.

5. Backing out: git merge --abort

Halfway through resolving, you realise the conflict is bigger than expected - a dozen files, all in code you do not understand - then do not push on. Retreat:

git merge --abort

The command runs silently, printing nothing - and the repo returns to exactly the state before you typed git merge, as if the merge had never started. Nothing is lost: both branches are intact, and you can read both sides properly and merge again once you understand them. Knowing this exit makes conflicts far less scary: the worst case is only "back to the starting line".

6. The data person's special pain: notebooks

An .ipynb file is JSON: each code cell is an array of strings, along with its output, a run counter (execution_count) and metadata. That makes notebook conflicts doubly painful:

  • Merely re-running the notebook - without editing a single line of code - changes outputs and execution_count, and the two branches now differ in a pile of meaningless places.
  • Conflict markers inserted into the middle of JSON make the file no longer valid JSON - Jupyter may refuse to open the very file you need to fix.
  • The diff of one code cell is buried in a forest of metadata, miserable to read by eye.

Three pain-relief tips, in order of worth:

  1. Clear outputs before committing (menu Edit → Clear All Outputs, or install a tool like nbstripout to do it automatically). The diff shrinks to real code, and phantom conflicts disappear.
  2. Move logic out into .py files - cleaning functions and feature functions live in src/, the notebook just imports and calls them. A conflict in a .py file is readable by eye, like the example above; what remains in the notebook leaves little to fight over.
  3. Avoid two people editing the same notebook at the same time - give each person their own notebook. The cheapest conflict resolution is not creating one.

Command reference

+--------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|       Command      |                                  What it does                                 |
+--------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| git merge <branch> | Merges a branch into the current one - stops and waits if there is a conflict |
| git status         | Shows which files await resolution (Unmerged paths)                           |
| git add <file>     | Marks a file as resolved                                                      |
| git commit         | Completes the merge once every conflicted file is added                       |
| git merge --abort  | Cancels the merge, back to the exact state before it                          |
+--------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Key points

A conflict is Git refusing to guess, not Git breaking. It only happens when two branches change the same line, and the referee must be you - because it is a business decision.

Resolved = final correct file + no markers left + git add + git commit. One leftover <<<<<<< in a Python file is a SyntaxError waiting to fire.

git merge --abort is always an exit. The worst state a conflict can put you in is "back to before the merge" - nothing to fear.

Notebook conflicts hurt because .ipynb is JSON. Clear outputs before committing, move logic into .py files, and keep two people out of one notebook.

Practice on your machine

Cause a real conflict yourself, resolve it by hand, then cause another one to practise the retreat - all in the practice repo ~/git-practice/sales-analysis; if you do not have it yet, create one quickly: mkdir -p ~/git-practice/sales-analysis && cd ~/git-practice/sales-analysis && git init && echo "date,amount" > sales.csv && git add . && git commit -m "init practice repo".

  1. Prepare a file with the line that will be disputed:
cd ~/git-practice/sales-analysis
git switch main
echo "THRESHOLD = 10" > config.txt
git add config.txt
git commit -m "add threshold config"
  1. On a new branch, lower the threshold:
git switch -c lower-threshold
echo "THRESHOLD = 5" > config.txt
git commit -am "lower threshold to 5"
  1. Back on main, change that SAME line the other way:
git switch main
echo "THRESHOLD = 20" > config.txt
git commit -am "raise threshold to 20"

The two branches now change the same line in two ways - everything a conflict needs.

  1. Merge to receive the conflict:
git merge lower-threshold

You must see CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in config.txt - Git stops and waits for your ruling.

  1. Look at the markers with your own eyes:
cat config.txt

The file must contain all three marker lines <<<<<<< HEAD, =======, >>>>>>> lower-threshold: the top part is THRESHOLD = 20 (main's version), the bottom is THRESHOLD = 5 (the version being merged in).

  1. Resolve by hand - decide 20 is correct, write the file into its final version (no markers) and seal it:
echo "THRESHOLD = 20" > config.txt
git add config.txt
git commit -m "Merge branch 'lower-threshold'"

The output [main ...] Merge branch 'lower-threshold' - the merge is complete, and history gains a merge commit.

  1. Cause a second conflict to practise backing out:
git switch -c wrong-units
echo "THRESHOLD = 1000" > config.txt
git commit -am "threshold in new units"
git switch main
echo "THRESHOLD = 25" > config.txt
git commit -am "tune threshold to 25"
git merge wrong-units

Again you see CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in config.txt, just like step 4.

  1. This time do not resolve - retreat:
git merge --abort
git status
cat config.txt

git status must report nothing to commit, working tree clean, and config.txt is back to THRESHOLD = 25 untouched - as if git merge had never been typed.

Self-check:

  • You can point at each part between the markers and name which branch it belongs to, without rereading the lesson.
  • After step 6, config.txt has no marker lines left and git log --oneline shows a merge commit on top.
  • After git merge --abort, the working tree is clean and the file is back to main's version - the exit always exists.

questions.prompt: Your repo holds 2 GB of data. When you run git switch -c try-log-transform, what actually happens on disk?

options.label: A
options.text: Git copies the entire working folder into a separate copy for the new branch

options.label: B
options.text: Git creates a new pointer at the current commit - just one extra file of a few dozen bytes

options.label: C
options.text: Git compresses the 2 GB of data and stores a snapshot for the branch

options.label: D
options.text: Nothing happens until you make your first commit on the new branch

questions.explanation: A branch in Git is only a pointer to a commit - inside .git it is a tiny file holding the hash of the commit it points at, so creating one is virtually free no matter how heavy the repo is. Answer a describes exactly the 'copy the folder to be safe' habit that branches were invented to replace - Git never copies the working folder. Answer c is also wrong because no extra snapshot is made: every commit already is a snapshot, and the branch merely points at one of them. Answer d fails on the word 'nothing': the new pointer, and HEAD moving onto it, happen immediately - the proof is that git branch lists the new branch with a * before you have committed anything.

questions.prompt: The experiment on try-log-transform worked, and you want to bring it into main. What is the correct way?

options.label: A
options.text: Stand on try-log-transform and run git merge main

options.label: B
options.text: Stand on main and run git merge try-log-transform

options.label: C
options.text: Stand on either branch - Git works out the direction by itself

options.label: D
options.text: Delete main and rename try-log-transform to main

questions.explanation: git merge pulls changes INTO the branch you are standing on, so the receiving branch - here, main - must be where you stand when you type the command. Answer a is the classic backwards merge: the command runs without any error, but the result is the opposite of what you wanted - main stays exactly as it was, while the experiment branch gets main mixed into it. Answer c is wrong because Git does not guess your intent: the direction is determined entirely by where you stand. Answer d 'works' in a literal sense but abuses the tool - you lose any history main gained after the split, and it is pointlessly convoluted when one merge in the right direction does the job.

questions.prompt: When is git merge a fast-forward (just sliding the pointer) instead of creating a merge commit?

options.label: A
options.text: When the two branches changed two different files and never touched the same line

options.label: B
options.text: When the receiving branch has had no new commits since the other branch split off

options.label: C
options.text: When the branch being merged has exactly one commit

options.label: D
options.text: When the merge produces no conflicts

questions.explanation: A fast-forward happens when the merged branch's history already contains the receiving branch's entire history - that is, the receiving branch has stood still since the split - so Git only needs to slide the pointer forward, creating no commit. Answers a and d confuse the fast-forward condition with the 'merges cleanly' condition: if both branches moved but changed different places, the merge is still smooth, yet Git must still create a two-parent merge commit because each side has commits the other lacks. Answer c is wrong because the number of commits on the branch is irrelevant - a ten-commit branch fast-forwards fine, as long as the receiving branch has not taken a single step.

questions.prompt: You open a file and see <<<<<<< HEAD ... ======= ... >>>>>>> fix-threshold. What do these markers mean, and what must you do once resolved?

options.label: A
options.text: The top part is from the branch you are standing on, the bottom from the branch being merged in; edit the file into its final correct version, delete all the markers, then git add + git commit

options.label: B
options.text: The top part is always the more correct one; just delete the bottom part and save, and the merge completes itself

options.label: C
options.text: It means the repo is corrupted; you need to re-clone and copy your changes over by hand

options.label: D
options.text: Keep all three marker lines in the file and git commit - Git picks the right version at commit time

questions.explanation: <<<<<<< HEAD down to ======= is the version from the branch you are standing on, and ======= down to >>>>>>> fix-threshold is from the branch being merged in; your job is to decide the final correct version (one side, both, or something new), delete every marker, then git add to mark the file resolved and git commit to complete the merge. Answer b is wrong twice: top-versus-bottom says nothing about right-versus-wrong - that is your business decision - and merely saving the file leaves it unmerged in Git's eyes; only git add + git commit finish the job. Answer c mistakes normal behaviour for disaster: a conflict is Git refusing to guess, the repo is perfectly healthy, and git merge --abort can even restore the pre-merge state. Answer d is the most dangerous - Git never picks for you, and leftover markers end up inside your code, where the next Python run raises a SyntaxError on that exact line.

questions.prompt: How does git branch -d differ from git branch -D?

options.label: A
options.text: -d deletes the local branch, -D also deletes it on the remote

options.label: B
options.text: -d refuses to delete an unmerged branch; -D force-deletes regardless

options.label: C
options.text: They are identical - -D is just an old spelling kept for compatibility

options.label: D
options.text: -D also erases all of the branch's commits from the repo immediately

questions.explanation: -d is the safe version: it checks whether the branch has been merged, and refuses with a hint if not - a guard rail so you cannot casually discard an experiment you never merged. -D skips that guard rail and deletes regardless. Answer a is wrong because both flags touch only the local branch - deleting a remote branch is a different command's job (git push --delete). Answer c is wrong because the two flags differ in exactly the place that matters most: the safety check. Answer d is wrong because deleting a branch deletes the label, not the commits: for a merged branch the commits still sit in main's history; for an unmerged branch killed with -D, the commits lose their name - hard to find again, but not erased immediately.

questions.prompt:
You type git merge fix-threshold and Git stops with CONFLICT. You open src/clean.py and see:


import pandas as pd

<<<<<<< HEAD
THRESHOLD = 20
=======
THRESHOLD = 5
>>>>>>> fix-threshold

def remove_outliers(df):
    return df[df["value"] < THRESHOLD]


You decide 20 is the correct threshold. Which sequence of next steps is CORRECT?

options.label: A
options.text: Delete the line THRESHOLD = 5, keep the three marker lines, then git commit - Git cleans up the markers at commit time

options.label: B
options.text: Edit the section between the markers into the single line THRESHOLD = 20, delete all three marker lines, then git add src/clean.py and git commit

options.label: C
options.text: Run git merge --abort - it finalises the merge and keeps main's THRESHOLD = 20

options.label: D
options.text: Run git commit -a right away without editing the file - HEAD is on main, so Git keeps the 20 and drops the 5

questions.explanation: Resolving a conflict is three mandatory steps: edit the file into its final correct version (here, the single line THRESHOLD = 20), delete all three marker lines, then git add to mark the file resolved and git commit to seal the merge - exactly answer b. Answer a is wrong because Git never cleans up markers: the three lines <<<<<<</=======/>>>>>>> would be committed verbatim into the middle of Python code, and the next run blows up with a SyntaxError right there. Answer c has --abort backwards: it finalises nothing - it cancels the whole merge and returns the repo to exactly the state before you typed git merge; it is the retreat, not the way to finish. Answer d is wrong in the most dangerous way: Git never picks a version for you. A bare git commit really is blocked (Committing is not possible because you have unmerged files), but adding -a tells Git to git add every tracked file for you - markers and all. The command goes through, and what lands in history is a merge commit carrying <<<<<<< in the middle of Python code. Do not count on Git to stop you: there is no shortcut around ruling by hand, only a shortcut that drags the markers into history.

questions.prompt:
You run git log --oneline --graph --all and get:


*   c2f8e5d (HEAD -> main) Merge branch 'add-readme'
|\
| * 8b1a4f6 (add-readme) add readme
* | 5d9c3e7 fix date parsing in loader
|/
| * 4f0a9d2 (try-dropout) try dropout layers
|/
* 7e4d1b8 train baseline model
* 9f3e2a1 initial notebook


Which branch HAS been fully merged into main, and which has NOT?

options.label: A
options.text: add-readme is merged, try-dropout is not - deleting try-dropout with git branch -d right now would be refused

options.label: B
options.text: Both are merged, because both appear in the log output

options.label: C
options.text: try-dropout is merged - its line joins the main line through the |/ mark

options.label: D
options.text: Neither is merged, because neither branch label sits on the same commit as main

questions.explanation: Read it off the graph: the top commit c2f8e5d is the merge commit Merge branch 'add-readme' with two parents - 8b1a4f6 of add-readme lies on one of the two lines converging into it, so all of add-readme is inside main's history. By contrast, no path leads down from main to 4f0a9d2 of try-dropout - that branch split off at 7e4d1b8 and went its own way, unmerged, so git branch -d try-dropout would refuse and hint at -D - answer a is right on both counts. Answer b is wrong because the --all flag shows EVERY branch regardless of merge state - appearing in the output says nothing. Answer c misreads the symbol: the |/ below 4f0a9d2 is where the branch SPLIT OFF from the main line at 7e4d1b8 (the common ancestor), not where it joined back - joining back would show as a merge commit ABOVE that branch, and try-dropout has none. Answer d is wrong because 'merged' means the branch's commits are reachable from main (inside its history), not that two labels sit on the same commit: after the merge commit, add-readme still sits at 8b1a4f6 yet is fully merged - git branch --merged would list it.

lessons.title: Remotes your repo lives in two places
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 22: Remotes your repo lives in two places

theory.contentHtml:
So far every commit, every branch, the entire history you have created lives in a .git folder on exactly one machine - yours. A dead hard drive wipes all of it, and a colleague who wants to see your code is out of luck. This lesson gives your repo a second home: a remote.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Everything lives on one machine
  2. Git is not GitHub
  3. A remote is a named other repo
  4. git clone - the whole history comes with it
  5. The other direction: pushing an existing repo
  6. Command reference
  7. Key points
  8. Practice on your machine

1. Everything lives on one machine

Git is a fully local tool. When you git commit, not a single byte leaves your machine - the commit is written into the .git folder sitting right next to your files. That is why committing is instant and works with no internet at all.

But local-only comes at two costs:

  • Lose the machine, lose everything. A failed drive, a stolen laptop, an accidental delete - your entire analysis history goes with it. For a data person, that can be three months of notebooks and cleaning scripts.
  • Nobody can work with you. A colleague who wants to rerun your script would have to - what, copy it over on a USB stick?

The answer to both: keep a copy of the repo somewhere else and synchronise with it. That somewhere else is called a remote.

2. Git is not GitHub

The two names get mixed up constantly, so let us separate them once and for all:

  • Git is version control software that runs on your machine - no internet, no account required.
  • GitHub (and GitLab, Bitbucket, …) is a service that hosts a copy of your repo on their servers, plus a web UI, pull requests, and issues.

GitHub does not own Git, and Git does not need GitHub. Delete your GitHub account and the repo on your machine keeps every single commit. Conversely, everything GitHub does - showing history, comparing branches - is just Git running on their servers.

For a data repo, which service you pick matters far less than understanding this: the repo up there is just a copy of yours, nothing more, nothing less.

3. A remote is a named other repo

To Git, a remote is simply another repo, given a name and an address. See which remotes the current repo knows about:

git remote -v

Output:

origin	https://github.com/xomdata/sales-analysis.git (fetch)
origin	https://github.com/xomdata/sales-analysis.git (push)

Reading it: this repo knows one remote named origin, pointing at an address on GitHub, used both for downloading (fetch) and for uploading (push).

origin is not a magic keyword - it is just the default name Git gives the first remote, the way a phone contact might be saved as "Home". You can rename it or add a second remote, but in practice one repo with one origin covers the vast majority of work.

A repo freshly created with git init prints nothing at all for git remote -v - until you declare one, Git has no idea any other repo exists.

4. git clone - the whole history comes with it

When the repo already exists on GitHub (your team's, or an open project), a single command brings it to your machine:

git clone https://github.com/xomdata/sales-analysis.git

Output:

Cloning into 'sales-analysis'...
remote: Enumerating objects: 127, done.
remote: Counting objects: 100% (127/127), done.
remote: Compressing objects: 100% (89/89), done.
remote: Total 127 (delta 41), reused 120 (delta 38), pack-reused 0
Receiving objects: 100% (127/127), 45.23 KiB | 1.20 MiB/s, done.
Resolving deltas: 100% (41/41), done.

clone does three things in one go:

  1. Creates a sales-analysis folder with the files at their latest version.
  2. Downloads the entire history - every commit, every branch, back to the very first one. Your copy is as complete as the one on the server; browsing the log or checking out an old commit needs no network.
  3. Sets up the remote origin, already pointing back at the address you cloned from.

Verify it:

cd sales-analysis
git log --oneline -3

Output:

e4f5a6b (HEAD -> main, origin/main) fix: handle missing values in revenue column
9c8d7e6 feat: add monthly revenue aggregation
a1b2c3d feat: initial cleaning script

The history is on your machine, and origin/main marks where the main branch stands on the remote side - a concept you will meet again throughout the next lesson.

5. The other direction: pushing an existing repo

And when you already have a local repo - say, the analysis project you have been committing to since the earlier modules - and now want it on GitHub? No cloning involved. The order is:

  1. On GitHub, create an empty repo (do not tick the option to add a README - the repo must be empty so the histories cannot clash).
  2. Back on your machine, declare that address as a remote:
git remote add origin git@github.com:duongdd/customer-churn.git
git remote -v

Output:

origin	git@github.com:duongdd/customer-churn.git (fetch)
origin	git@github.com:duongdd/customer-churn.git (push)
  1. Push the history up for the first time:
git push -u origin main

Output:

Enumerating objects: 15, done.
Counting objects: 100% (15/15), done.
Delta compression using up to 8 threads
Compressing objects: 100% (12/12), done.
Writing objects: 100% (15/15), 4.28 KiB | 1.42 MiB/s, done.
Total 15 (delta 2), reused 0 (delta 0), pack-reused 0
remote: Resolving deltas: 100% (2/2), done.
To github.com:duongdd/customer-churn.git
 * [new branch]      main -> main
branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.

The -u flag gets dissected in the next lesson; for now it is enough to know it makes every later git push shorter.

The most important idea of the whole lesson sits right here: after connecting the remote, the two repos still do NOT synchronise on their own. Commit ten more times and GitHub sits unchanged. Every exchange between local and remote is an explicit command you type - push, pull, fetch - and that is exactly what the next lesson is about.

Command reference

+-------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|            Command            |                                  What it does                                 |
+-------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| git clone <url>               | Copies a repo to your machine with its entire history, sets up remote origin  |
| git remote -v                 | Lists the declared remotes with their addresses                               |
| git remote add origin <url>   | Connects an existing local repo to a remote repo                              |
| git remote rename <old> <new> | Renames a remote                                                              |
| git remote remove <name>      | Removes a remote from the address book (deletes nothing on the server)        |
| git push -u origin main       | Pushes the main branch to the remote for the first time (details next lesson) |
+-------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Key points

Git ≠ GitHub. Git is software on your machine; GitHub is a service hosting a copy of the repo. Delete the GitHub account and the local repo keeps everything.

A remote is just another repo with a name. There is nothing mystical about origin - it is the default name for the first remote, and git remote -v shows it any time.

clone brings back the ENTIRE history, not just the latest version. After cloning, browsing the log and checking out old commits works fully offline.

Local and remote never synchronise by themselves. Committing does not mean GitHub has it. Every exchange is an explicit command - and that is a feature, not a gap: you decide exactly what leaves your machine, and when.

Practice on your machine

This section needs a GitHub account - free, sign up at github.com/signup if you do not have one yet. You will connect the practice repo ~/git-practice/sales-analysis from the earlier modules to GitHub, then try cloning a public repo into a different folder (if you do not have the practice repo yet, create it quickly: mkdir -p ~/git-practice/sales-analysis, then git init inside it and commit any file).

  1. On GitHub click New repository, name it sales-analysis, and leave the repo completely empty - do not tick the options to add a README or .gitignore.

  2. Back on your machine, declare that address as the remote (replace <your-username> with your GitHub username):

cd ~/git-practice/sales-analysis
git remote add origin https://github.com/<your-username>/sales-analysis.git

The command prints nothing at all - with Git, silence means success.

  1. Check the remote address book:
git remote -v

You must see exactly two lines, same address, one (fetch) and one (push):

origin	https://github.com/<your-username>/sales-analysis.git (fetch)
origin	https://github.com/<your-username>/sales-analysis.git (push)
  1. Now the other direction - clone any public repo into a DIFFERENT folder (do not clone inside the practice repo). For example GitHub's classic Hello-World repo:
cd ~/git-practice
git clone https://github.com/octocat/Hello-World.git

You must see Cloning into 'Hello-World'... and the object-counting lines running up to 100%.

  1. Enter the folder you just cloned and verify that both the history and the remote came pre-set:
cd Hello-World
git log --oneline -3
git remote -v

git log prints other people's commits - the entire history is now on your machine; git remote -v shows origin already pointing back at the address you cloned from, with no remote add on your part.

Self-check:

  • git remote -v in the practice repo prints exactly 2 origin lines - one (fetch), one (push).
  • You can explain why the repo created on GitHub must stay empty (no README ticked).
  • Inside the cloned folder, git log browses the full history with no network at all.
  • You can say when to use git clone and when to use git remote add (no local repo yet / existing local repo).
