lessons.title: Two-way sync push, pull, fetch
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 23: Two-way sync push, pull, fetch

theory.contentHtml:
You now have two repos - one on your machine, one on GitHub - and you know they do not talk to each other on their own. This lesson is the entire "language" between the two sides: sending up, bringing down, and dealing with the moment they diverge.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Sending commits up with git push
  2. The first push: -u sets the upstream
  3. git fetch - download without touching your files
  4. git pull = fetch + merge
  5. When a push is rejected
  6. A healthy sync routine
  7. Command reference
  8. Key points
  9. Practice on your machine

1. Sending commits up with git push

git push sends the commits the remote does not have yet from your machine to the remote:

git push

Output:

Enumerating objects: 5, done.
Counting objects: 100% (5/5), done.
Delta compression using up to 8 threads
Compressing objects: 100% (3/3), done.
Writing objects: 100% (3/3), 342 bytes | 342.00 KiB/s, done.
Total 3 (delta 1), reused 0 (delta 0), pack-reused 0
remote: Resolving deltas: 100% (1/1), completed with 1 local object.
To github.com:duongdd/customer-churn.git
   a1b2c3d..e4f5a6b  main -> main

The last line is the one worth reading: the remote's main branch just advanced from commit a1b2c3d to e4f5a6b - exactly where you are standing. Push only sends the difference, so if you commit regularly, each push is a few KB, never a re-upload of the whole repo.

2. The first push: -u sets the upstream

For the first push of a branch, though, Git does not yet know which branch on the remote this local branch corresponds to. You say it explicitly, once:

git push -u origin main

Output:

Enumerating objects: 15, done.
Counting objects: 100% (15/15), done.
Delta compression using up to 8 threads
Compressing objects: 100% (12/12), done.
Writing objects: 100% (15/15), 4.28 KiB | 1.42 MiB/s, done.
Total 15 (delta 2), reused 0 (delta 0), pack-reused 0
remote: Resolving deltas: 100% (2/2), done.
To github.com:duongdd/customer-churn.git
 * [new branch]      main -> main
branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.

The -u flag (long form: --set-upstream) records the link: "local branch main tracks origin/main". That link is called the upstream, and thanks to it:

  • From now on a bare git push and git pull are enough - Git knows where to send to and where to take from.
  • git status starts comparing the two sides for you:
git status

Output:

On branch main
Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 1 commit.
  (use "git push" to publish your local commits)

nothing to commit, working tree clean

"Ahead by 1 commit" - you have one commit the remote does not. Without an upstream, git status cannot say that sentence. Set it once per branch and you are done; in a repo obtained via clone, main comes with it already set.

3. git fetch - download without touching your files

git fetch downloads every new commit from the remote onto your machine, but - and this is the crux - changes none of the files you are working on:

git fetch

Output:

remote: Enumerating objects: 5, done.
remote: Counting objects: 100% (5/5), done.
remote: Compressing objects: 100% (2/2), done.
remote: Total 3 (delta 1), reused 3 (delta 1), pack-reused 0
Unpacking objects: 100% (3/3), 1.01 KiB | 1.01 MiB/s, done.
From github.com:xomdata/sales-analysis
   a1b2c3d..e4f5a6b  main       -> origin/main

The new commits are now on your machine, but all they moved is origin/main - the marker for "where the remote's main branch stands". Your own main, and every file in your folder, stay exactly still.

That makes fetch unconditionally safe, and the way to preview what your colleagues just did:

git log --oneline origin/main

Output:

e4f5a6b (origin/main) fix: handle missing values in revenue column
9c8d7e6 feat: add monthly revenue aggregation
a1b2c3d (HEAD -> main) feat: add churn features

Reading it: origin/main stands two commits ahead of you - a fix and a revenue aggregation feature. You know precisely what is about to enter your machine before letting it mix into your work.

4. git pull = fetch + merge

When you do want to receive the changes for real, use git pull. It is exactly two steps rolled into one: fetch (download the new commits) then merge (fold them into your current branch):

git pull

Output:

Updating a1b2c3d..e4f5a6b
Fast-forward
 clean_data.py | 12 ++++++++++++
 1 file changed, 12 insertions(+)

"Fast-forward" means you had no diverging commits of your own, so Git simply wound your branch forward - nothing needed merging. The file clean_data.py in your folder has genuinely changed now: 12 lines from your colleague were added.

When both sides do have their own commits, pull creates a merge commit - the same merging and conflict handling you learned in the branching module, nothing new to memorise.

5. When a push is rejected

Sooner or later you will hit this - a push bounced back:

git push

Output:

To github.com:xomdata/sales-analysis.git
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to 'github.com:xomdata/sales-analysis.git'
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not
hint: have locally. This is usually caused by another repository pushing to
hint: the same ref. If you want to first integrate the remote changes, use
hint: 'git pull ...' before pushing again.

Do not panic - read closely and Git has already said everything: the remote has commits you do not have (a colleague pushed before you did). If Git accepted your push anyway, their commits would be overwritten. This kind of rejection is called non-fast-forward: your history is not a simple continuation of the history on the remote.

There is exactly one correct fix, and it is gentler than the error message looks:

git pull
git push

pull brings their commits down and merges them with yours; push again and you are done.

There is one more "fix" Git will not stop you from forcing: git push --force. It makes the remote accept your history by throwing away other people's commits - on a shared branch, that is the fastest way to erase hours of a colleague's work without a trace. Never force push to a shared branch. Catching yourself about to type --force to "get past the error" is the signal to stop and git pull instead.

6. A healthy sync routine

The mechanics are covered; what remains is rhythm:

  • Pull before you start the working day. Open the laptop, git pull, then code. Starting from the latest version means far fewer conflicts all day.
  • Push when a piece of work is done. Done meaning meaningful - the script runs, the analysis produces numbers - then commit and push. From that second your work lives in two places: a dead machine loses nothing, and colleagues see it immediately.
  • The longer the two sides drift, the worse the merge. Let them diverge for a week and the Friday pull becomes a pile of conflicts - with notebooks, an especially painful pile. Syncing in short beats is nearly free; syncing in long beats always comes with a bill.

Command reference

+-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|            Command            |                                What it does                               |
+-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| git push                      | Sends local commits the remote lacks up to the remote (needs an upstream) |
| git push -u origin main       | First push of a branch: pushes and sets the upstream                      |
| git fetch                     | Downloads new commits from the remote, does NOT touch your working files  |
| git log --oneline origin/main | Inspects the remote-side history after a fetch - look before you take     |
| git pull                      | fetch + merge: download and fold into the current branch                  |
| git status                    | With an upstream, reports how many commits you are ahead/behind           |
+-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Key points

fetch previews, pull receives. fetch downloads commits without changing any of your files; pull = fetch + merge - the files in your folder genuinely change.

-u is needed once per branch. It sets the upstream so that bare git push/git pull suffice, and git status can tell you how far ahead/behind you are.

A rejected push is not your mistake - it is a message. The remote has commits you lack. git pull, then push again. That is everyday teamwork.

Never force push to a shared branch. --force makes the remote discard other people's commits to accept yours. On your own private branch it occasionally has its place; on a shared branch it is an accident waiting to happen.

Practice on your machine

This section needs a GitHub account (free - github.com/signup) and the practice repo ~/git-practice/sales-analysis with the remote connected in the previous lesson. You will push for the first time, create a commit "by someone else" by editing a file right on the GitHub web UI, then live through the full cycle yourself: fetch → pull, and a rejected push → pull → push.

  1. Push the history up for the first time:
cd ~/git-practice/sales-analysis
git push -u origin main

You must see * [new branch] main -> main and the line branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.. If Git stops to ask you to sign in, follow the prompt it shows (usually a browser window); if you get stuck at authentication entirely, that is exactly the topic of the next lesson - do that one first and come back here.

  1. Create a commit only the remote has: open the repo on the GitHub web UI, click README.md (or any file), click the pencil icon to edit, add a line, and press Commit changes. GitHub just created a commit directly on the server - exactly like a colleague pushing before you.

  2. Back on your machine, download without merging - look first:

git fetch
git log --oneline origin/main -3

The fetch output must contain a main -> origin/main line, and the log shows origin/main standing exactly one commit ahead of you - the commit you just made on the web. The files on your machine have not changed at all.

  1. Now receive it for real:
git pull

You must see Fast-forward - open the file, and the line edited on the web is now on your machine.

  1. Recreate the rejected-push scene: edit the file on the GitHub web UI once more (repeat step 2), then on your machine make a local commit WITHOUT pulling first:
echo "local note" >> notes.md
git add notes.md
git commit -m "docs: add local note"
git push

The push must bounce back with ! [rejected] main -> main (fetch first) plus the hint lines - the two sides have diverged, exactly the non-fast-forward scene from the lesson.

  1. Fix it by the book:
git pull --no-edit
git push

--no-edit merely accepts the default merge message so no editor opens. This push must go through cleanly - open GitHub on the web and you see both the web-edit commit and your local commit.

Self-check:

  • git status prints Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'..
  • You have seen the ! [rejected] ... (fetch first) output with your own eyes and resolved it with pull → push, never touching --force.
  • You can point at the exact difference between step 3 (fetch - files stand still) and step 4 (pull - files genuinely change).
  • The history on the GitHub web UI shows both the web-edit commit and the docs: add local note commit.

lessons.title: Signing in to GitHub SSH keys and tokens
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 27: Signing in to GitHub SSH keys and tokens

theory.contentHtml:
The first time you push to GitHub, odds are you get stopped for authentication - and typing your account password gets you rejected outright. That is not you doing it wrong; GitHub means it. This lesson sets up, once and properly, the two ways in: SSH keys and Personal Access Tokens.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Why your password stopped working
  2. Creating an SSH key
  3. Adding the public key to GitHub and testing
  4. Two kinds of URL: HTTPS and SSH
  5. Personal Access Tokens
  6. Command reference
  7. Key points
  8. Practice on your machine

1. Why your password stopped working

Since August 2021, GitHub has dropped password authentication entirely for Git operations over HTTPS. The reason is easy to see: a password is a single string that opens every door of the account, one leak loses everything - and people paste it everywhere.

Two ways in remain:

  • SSH keys - a cryptographic key pair; your machine keeps one half, GitHub the other. Set up once, and push/pull never prompts you again. This is the road to take for your main working machine.
  • Personal Access Token (PAT) - a secret string used in place of the password over HTTPS, with limitable permissions and an expiry date. Right for a borrowed machine, CI, or wherever SSH is not an option.

Most of this lesson is about SSH, because once it is set up you get to forget it exists.

2. Creating an SSH key

One command, run on your machine:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"

Output:

Generating public/private ed25519 key pair.
Enter file in which to save the key (/home/duong/.ssh/id_ed25519):
Enter passphrase (empty for no passphrase):
Enter same passphrase again:
Your identification has been saved in /home/duong/.ssh/id_ed25519
Your public key has been saved in /home/duong/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
The key fingerprint is:
SHA256:Xr4beV0y6dQmMxTubXcCFg3zk8lQnDpRy2t1sHaVOkE you@example.com

Pressing Enter through the prompts is fine (an empty passphrase is convenient; setting one adds a layer of safety). -t ed25519 picks the modern algorithm; -C is merely a comment label - use your email so you can tell later whose key it is.

The command produces a pair of files:

  • ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 - the private key. The secret half. This file never leaves your machine: not sent over chat, not pasted on the web, not committed into a repo. Whoever holds it becomes you in GitHub's eyes.
  • ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub - the public key (note the .pub suffix). The public half, born to be given away: you hand it to GitHub, and anyone seeing it is harmless.

The mechanism underneath: what one half encrypts, only the other half can decrypt. GitHub holds the public key, and your machine proves it holds the matching private key - without ever sending the private key anywhere.

3. Adding the public key to GitHub and testing

Print the public key:

cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

Output:

ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIN8xX2mZq7cRkA5uFdWqJhTsK9vLmPnE4gYwBoC1rDaU you@example.com

Copy that whole line, go to GitHub: Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key, paste it into the Key box, give it a name that identifies the machine ("work-laptop"), and save. Then test end to end:

ssh -T git@github.com

Output:

Hi duongdd! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access.

On the very first connection SSH will additionally ask Are you sure you want to continue connecting? because it has never met this server - type yes. And the "does not provide shell access" line looks like an error but is the success: GitHub confirms it recognised you (your own username after Hi), it just will not open a shell - which was never what we wanted anyway.

4. Two kinds of URL: HTTPS and SSH

The same repo on GitHub has two addresses, and the address determines the authentication:

https://github.com/xomdata/sales-analysis.git    ← HTTPS form → asks for username + token (PAT)
git@github.com:xomdata/sales-analysis.git        ← SSH form   → uses the key pair you just made

This is the classic stumble: SSH key fully installed, and pushing still asks for a password - because the repo was cloned with the HTTPS-form URL, so Git takes the HTTPS road and never so much as glances at the key. Authentication follows the URL, not whatever you have installed on the machine.

Check which form the repo is using:

git remote -v

Output:

origin	https://github.com/xomdata/sales-analysis.git (fetch)
origin	https://github.com/xomdata/sales-analysis.git (push)

Starts with https:// - this repo takes the HTTPS road. To switch it to the SSH key, change the remote's address (this only edits the local "address book"; it touches neither history nor the server):

git remote set-url origin git@github.com:xomdata/sales-analysis.git
git remote -v

Output:

origin	git@github.com:xomdata/sales-analysis.git (fetch)
origin	git@github.com:xomdata/sales-analysis.git (push)

From now on, every push/pull of this repo goes through the SSH key - no more prompts.

5. Personal Access Tokens

When you still need the HTTPS road - a borrowed machine, a notebook on a server, CI - the thing you type into the password prompt is a PAT, created under Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens. Three principles when creating one:

  • Pick fine-grained over the classic kind: you can limit which repos this token opens and what it may do (read-only, or read-write content). If the token leaks, the damage is contained.
  • Set an expiry. 90 days is reasonable. An expired token dies on its own - even one you forgot existed cannot become a permanent back door.
  • Treat the token exactly like a password. It is a string standing in for the password, so every password discipline applies to it. Data people have one trap of their own here: never paste a token into a notebook. The cell git clone https://TOKEN@github.com/... finishes running and stays in the .ipynb file; the notebook gets committed, and the token becomes part of the repo history - where everyone can read it and git rm cannot remove it (that is history: deleting the current file leaves the old commits intact). If a token does leak, go to GitHub and revoke it immediately - this is the moment you appreciate the expiry and the narrow permissions.

Command reference

+--------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                   Command                  |                                What it does                                |
+--------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com" | Creates the SSH key pair (private + public) in ~/.ssh/                     |
| cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub                  | Prints the public key for copying into GitHub                              |
| ssh -T git@github.com                      | Tests whether GitHub recognises the key                                    |
| git remote -v                              | Inspects the remote URL - https:// vs git@ reveals the authentication road |
| git remote set-url origin <url>            | Changes the remote's address (e.g. switching HTTPS → SSH)                  |
+--------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Key points

Your account password no longer works for Git operations. Since 2021, the HTTPS road needs a PAT - or switch to an SSH key altogether.

The private key never leaves the machine. The .pub file is born to be given away; the file without .pub goes nowhere and gets committed nowhere, in any form.

Authentication follows the remote's URL. Cloned via https:// means token prompts, git@ means the key - if you installed an SSH key and still get password prompts, check git remote -v and switch with git remote set-url.

A PAT is a password with an expiry date - and a secret all the same. Create it fine-grained, narrow, expiring. Never paste it into a notebook: a token inside a committed .ipynb lives in the repo history forever.

Practice on your machine

This section needs a GitHub account (free - github.com/signup) and the practice repo ~/git-practice/sales-analysis already on GitHub from the previous two lessons. You will create an SSH key, hand the public half to GitHub, switch the remote to the SSH form, and push without typing anything.

  1. Create the key pair (replace the email with yours, press Enter through the prompts):
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"

You must see Your public key has been saved in ...id_ed25519.pub along with a SHA256:... fingerprint.

  1. Print the public key to copy it:
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

Exactly one line starting with ssh-ed25519 - copy that whole line. (Remember: the file with the .pub suffix is the one born to be given away; the file without .pub stays put on your machine.)

  1. On GitHub: Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key, paste it into the Key box, give it a name that identifies the machine ("my-laptop"), and save.

  2. Test end to end:

ssh -T git@github.com

On the first connection SSH asks Are you sure you want to continue connecting? - type yes. You must see Hi <your-username>! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access. - it looks like an error but is the success.

  1. Switch the practice repo's remote to the SSH form:
cd ~/git-practice/sales-analysis
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:<your-username>/sales-analysis.git
git remote -v

The two lines must now start with git@github.com: instead of https://:

origin	git@github.com:<your-username>/sales-analysis.git (fetch)
origin	git@github.com:<your-username>/sales-analysis.git (push)
  1. Try a push - this time nothing may prompt you:
git push

Seeing Everything up-to-date (or a normal push run if there are new commits) with no username/password question means you are done - from now on every push/pull of this repo goes through the SSH key.

Self-check:

  • ssh -T git@github.com greets your exact GitHub username.
  • git remote -v prints 2 lines in the git@github.com: form, no more https://.
  • git push runs straight through, asking for no username/password.
  • What you pasted into GitHub is the content of the .pub file - the private key never left the machine.

questions.prompt: How do Git and GitHub differ?

options.label: A
options.text: They are the same thing - GitHub is Git's full name

options.label: B
options.text: Git is version control software running on your machine; GitHub is a service hosting a copy of the repo on a server

options.label: C
options.text: Git is for code, GitHub is for data

options.label: D
options.text: GitHub is the paid edition, Git is the free one

questions.explanation: Git is software that runs entirely on your machine - commits, branches and history all work with no internet and no account. GitHub (like GitLab and Bitbucket) is a service that HOSTS a copy of the repo, plus a web UI, pull requests and issues. Delete your GitHub account and the local repo keeps every single commit - proof enough that the two are independent. They are not one thing (a), there is no code/data split (c) - both manage files of any kind, and GitHub is not a paid edition of Git (d): Git is free open-source software, while GitHub has both free and paid plans but is a separate service company.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?

options.label: A
options.text: Nothing - two names for the same command

options.label: B
options.text: fetch downloads new commits without touching your working files; pull = fetch + merge into the current branch

options.label: C
options.text: fetch downloads only the newest commit, pull downloads the whole history

options.label: D
options.text: pull only previews, while fetch actually merges the changes in

questions.explanation: fetch downloads every new commit onto your machine but only moves the origin/main marker - your own branch and every file in your folder stay exactly still, which makes it unconditionally safe and the way to preview what colleagues just did (git log --oneline origin/main). pull is precisely two steps in one: fetch then merge - after a pull, the files in your folder have genuinely changed. Answer d states the two roles exactly backwards - mixing up that direction is the source of many surprises. And c gets the mechanism wrong: both download all the commits the remote has that you lack; the difference is whether they get merged into your branch.

questions.prompt: git push returns ! [rejected] main -> main (fetch first). What is the correct fix?

options.label: A
options.text: git push --force to make the remote accept it

options.label: B
options.text: Delete the repo and clone it again from scratch

options.label: C
options.text: git pull to bring the remote's commits down and merge them with yours, then push again

options.label: D
options.text: Rename the local branch and push it under a different name

questions.explanation: A non-fast-forward rejection means the remote has commits you do not have - usually a colleague pushed first. Git refuses in order to protect those commits from being overwritten. The correct fix is gentler than the error looks: git pull (bring their commits down and merge with yours), then git push again. --force (a) is the most dangerous answer: it makes the remote throw away other people's commits to accept your history - on a shared branch, that erases a colleague's work without a trace. Deleting and re-cloning (b) loses your own unpushed local commits too. Renaming the branch (d) will upload, but as a stray new branch - it does nothing to actually combine the two people's work.

questions.prompt: You just finished a git commit. If a colleague opens GitHub, do they see that commit?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes - commits synchronise to the remote the moment they are created

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, but only after GitHub's periodic scan, a few minutes later

options.label: C
options.text: No - the commit exists only on your machine until you git push

options.label: D
options.text: It depends - if the repo was created via git clone, commits synchronise automatically

questions.explanation: Git is a local tool: git commit writes into the .git folder on your machine, and not a single byte leaves it. Local and remote do NOT synchronise on their own - every exchange is an explicit command you type (push, pull, fetch). For a colleague to see it, you must git push. There is no hidden sync mechanism (a), GitHub cannot scan your machine and has no access to it anyway (b), and clone merely pre-configures the origin remote and the upstream for shorter commands - it enables no auto-sync mode (d). This is a feature, not a gap: you decide exactly what leaves your machine, and when.

questions.prompt: You installed an SSH key and ssh -T git@github.com greets you by name, yet git push still asks for a username/password. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The SSH key has expired and must be regenerated

options.label: B
options.text: The repo's remote is an https://-form URL, so Git takes the HTTPS road and never uses the key - check with git remote -v, switch with git remote set-url

options.label: C
options.text: The private key must also be uploaded to GitHub before pushing works

options.label: D
options.text: GitHub requires a password on the first push of every repo

questions.explanation: Authentication follows the remote's URL, not whatever you have installed on the machine: cloned via https://github.com/... means Git takes the HTTPS road and asks for a token, while git@github.com:... takes the SSH road and uses the key. ssh -T greeting you by name proves the key works fine - the only problem is that this repo does not travel that road. Check git remote -v; if you see https://, then git remote set-url origin git@github.com:user/repo.git and you are done. SSH keys do not expire (a) - expiry is a PAT concept. Answer c violates the single biggest rule of the lesson: the private key NEVER leaves your machine - what you give GitHub is the public key (the .pub file). And d does not exist: GitHub actually dropped password authentication altogether back in 2021.

questions.prompt:
You run git push and get back:


To github.com:xomdata/sales-analysis.git
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to 'github.com:xomdata/sales-analysis.git'
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not
hint: have locally. This is usually caused by another repository pushing to
hint: the same ref. If you want to first integrate the remote changes, use
hint: 'git pull ...' before pushing again.


Read the state: what is happening, and what is the correct next command?

options.label: A
options.text: The network dropped mid-push and it failed - typing git push again fixes it

options.label: B
options.text: The remote has commits your machine does not (non-fast-forward) - run git pull to merge them down, then git push again

options.label: C
options.text: You lack write access to this repo - you must ask the repo owner for write permission

options.label: D
options.text: The remote main branch is protected - open the repo Settings, unprotect it, then push again

questions.explanation: The hint lines say it verbatim: 'the remote contains work that you do not have locally' - the remote has commits you lack, usually because someone (or you yourself, editing on the web) pushed first. This is a non-fast-forward rejection, and the hint even prescribes the cure: 'git pull ... before pushing again' - pull to merge, then push again (b). Retyping git push (a) is pointless: with the state on both sides unchanged, the next attempt produces the exact same error - rejected is not a network failure; a network failure shows 'Could not resolve host' or a timeout, with no [rejected] in sight. Missing write access (c) looks entirely different - 'Permission denied' or an HTTP 403 - not [rejected] ... (fetch first). A protected branch (d) is refused with a different message too ('protected branch hook declined'), and nobody has enabled protection on your own practice repo. Reading the message precisely is what separates these three error classes without guessing.

questions.prompt:
On a new machine, you run two commands and see:


$ git remote -v
origin	git@github.com:xomdata/sales-analysis.git (fetch)
origin	git@github.com:xomdata/sales-analysis.git (push)
$ git push
git@github.com: Permission denied (publickey).
fatal: Could not read from remote repository.

Please make sure you have the correct access rights
and the repository exists.


What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: The remote URL is the wrong form - it must be switched to https:// before pushing works

options.label: B
options.text: The repo does not exist on GitHub - the line 'and the repository exists' says so

options.label: C
options.text: GitHub does not recognise any SSH key from this machine - test with ssh -T git@github.com; a new machine with no key yet needs ssh-keygen, then paste the .pub file into GitHub

options.label: D
options.text: Your GitHub login session expired - sign in again on github.com, then push

questions.explanation: git remote -v shows the remote in the git@github.com: form - this repo takes the SSH road, meaning authentication by key pair. Permission denied (publickey) means the server refused every key this machine offered: on a NEW machine that usually simply means no key exists yet (~/.ssh is empty), or a key exists but its public half was never added to the GitHub account - the proper procedure is to probe with ssh -T git@github.com, then ssh-keygen and paste the .pub file into GitHub (c). Switching to https:// (a) dodges SSH but treats the symptom: you would then need a PAT, while nothing is wrong with the SSH-form URL - what is missing is the key. The line 'and the repository exists' (b) is boilerplate printed for EVERY failed connection - authentication died before Git could even check whether the repo exists, so it proves nothing. And d does not exist: Git operations over SSH never use the web login session, and GitHub dropped passwords for Git operations back in 2021.

lessons.title: Pull requests where code gets read before it lands
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 29: Pull requests where code gets read before it lands

theory.contentHtml:
Working alone, you fold a branch into main with a single git merge - nobody asks questions. On a team it is different: code must be read by someone else before it reaches main, and the place where that happens is the pull request.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. A PR is a proposal, not a git command
  2. The life of a pull request
  3. Review: reading the diff, commenting line by line
  4. What makes a good PR
  5. Reviewing data work
  6. Merge commit or squash
  7. Command reference
  8. Key points
  9. Practice on your machine

1. A PR is a proposal, not a git command

Try typing:

git pull-request

Output:

git: 'pull-request' is not a git command. See 'git --help'.

No such command. Pull requests do not belong to Git - they are a GitHub feature (GitLab calls them merge requests), built on top of the branch concept that Git provides. Git knows branches and merges; "proposing", "discussing" and "approving" are the hosting platform's business.

Read the name literally: "I propose that you pull this branch into main". A PR is three things:

  • A diff - the full difference between your branch and main, shown line by line.
  • A place to talk - a description, comments, and comments attached to individual lines of code.
  • A merge button - pressed only once the team agrees (and usually once someone has approved).

In other words: the PR stands between "I finished writing it" and "it is on main". That gap is exactly where bugs get stopped.

2. The life of a pull request

It starts by pushing the branch to GitHub:

git push -u origin an/clean-revenue-column

Output:

Enumerating objects: 5, done.
...
remote: Create a pull request for 'an/clean-revenue-column' on GitHub by visiting:
remote:      https://github.com/xom-data/revenue-report/pull/new/an/clean-revenue-column
To github.com:xom-data/revenue-report.git
 * [new branch]      an/clean-revenue-column -> an/clean-revenue-column

Git prints the link for you - GitHub has noticed the new branch and invites you to open a PR. The full life cycle:

  1. Push the branch to GitHub.
  2. Open pull request - pick the source branch (compare) and the target branch (base, usually main).
  3. Write the description - what, why, and how you tested it.
  4. The reviewer reads the diff and comments on any line that looks off.
  5. You address the feedback - fix the code, commit, and push to the same branch. The PR updates itself; no new PR needed.
  6. The reviewer approves → merge on GitHub with the button, not with a git merge on your machine.

A decent PR description looks like this:

## What

Standardise the revenue column: strip currency symbols, cast to float.

## Why

The monthly report sums revenue as text - the March total came out wrong.

## How tested

Re-ran the pipeline on March data; the total now matches finance's number.

Three sentences, but the reviewer now knows exactly where to look and how much to trust.

3. Review: reading the diff, commenting line by line

On the PR page, the Files changed tab shows the diff of every file. Hovering over any line lets the reviewer comment on that exact line:

revenue = revenue.replace("$", "")

"The March data also has € symbols - replacing only $ will miss rows. Maybe a regex that strips everything that isn't a digit or a dot?"

Comments pinned to lines of code are the PR's killer feature: the feedback sits right next to the thing it is about, instead of a chat message saying "the revenue calc looks wrong somewhere" followed by both of you hunting for "somewhere".

At the end of a review pass, the reviewer picks one of two:

  • Approve - good to go into main.
  • Request changes - needs fixing first.

You fix, commit, push. The PR refreshes its diff and the old discussion stays in place - anyone arriving later can read the whole story: the original proposal, the feedback, and how the code changed.

4. What makes a good PR

The most-quoted law of the trade: a 400-line PR gets a careful review, a 2000-line PR gets an "LGTM" (looks good to me). Reviewers are human - the longer the diff, the more the eyes skim.

Three properties of a good PR:

  • Small - tens to a few hundred lines. Small enough to read in one sitting.
  • One topic - if you are fixing the revenue logic, do not also rename 15 variables in another file along the way. That work deserves its own PR, where it gets read for what it is.
  • A description that says WHY and how it was tested - the diff already says what changed; what it cannot say is why the change was needed, and which data you tried it on.

What about big jobs? Split them. "Rework the revenue pipeline" splits into: a PR that cleans up column names → a PR that fixes the calculation → a PR that adds a validation step. Each PR stands on its own, and main still works after every merge.

5. Reviewing data work

Your reviewer wants to see the data transformation logic: which rows get filtered, whether that join drops records, whether the formula is right. What they do not want: scrolling past 500 lines of notebook output - result tables, chart images - wedged between the lines of code they need to read.

A notebook full of output makes a shredded diff: every re-run changes the outputs, and the diff balloons with noise even when the logic did not change one word (the lesson Notebooks and large data in Git dissects this properly). Before opening a PR that contains a notebook:

  • Clear all outputs - the diff shrinks to code, and the reviewer can actually read it.
  • Logic you use repeatedly (cleaning functions, metric calculations) gradually moves into .py files - plain text, clean diffs, easy review.

A good reviewer will ask data questions: "is that join inner or left - if customers without orders vanish, is the total still right?". For them to get that far, the diff has to be clean enough to reach the logic.

6. Merge commit or squash

When you press the merge button on GitHub, you choose how to fold the branch in:

  • Create a merge commit - keeps every commit from the branch and adds one merge commit marking the join. main's history keeps full detail - including every "fix typo" and "wip" commit made along the way.
  • Squash and merge - compresses the whole branch into exactly one commit on main. Ten scrappy branch commits become one tidily named commit, for example clean revenue column (#12).

Many teams pick squash because it keeps main's history lean: each commit on main = one reviewed PR. Reading git log on main reads like a list of finished changes, not everyone's rough-draft diary.

The trade-off: the individual branch commits never reach main - so after a squash merge, delete the branch (GitHub offers a delete button right after merging); its job is done.

Command reference

This lesson is light on commands and heavy on concepts - so a term reference:

+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|          Term         |                                                    Meaning                                                    |
+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Pull Request (PR)     | A proposal to merge a branch into main, with a diff + a place to discuss. A GitHub feature, not a git command |
| base / compare        | The target branch (usually main) / the source branch holding your changes                                     |
| Files changed         | The tab showing the PR's whole diff, where line comments live                                                 |
| Approve               | The reviewer agrees to merge                                                                                  |
| Request changes       | The reviewer wants fixes before merging                                                                       |
| Create a merge commit | Merge keeping every branch commit + one added merge commit                                                    |
| Squash and merge      | Compress the whole branch into one commit on main - lean history                                              |
| LGTM                  | "Looks good to me" - and on an oversized PR, usually a sign nobody really read it                             |
+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Key points

A PR is a GitHub feature, not a git command. Git provides branches and merging; the "propose - read - approve" part lives on the hosting platform.

Pushing more commits to the same branch updates the PR. Feedback does not mean a new PR - fix, commit, push, and the old discussion stays where it was.

Small PR, one topic, a description that says WHY. The diff already says "what"; the description must answer "why" and "how was it tested" - the two things a reviewer cannot infer.

For notebooks: clear outputs before opening the PR. The reviewer needs to read transformation logic, not scroll past 500 lines of result tables.

Practice on your machine

This section needs a GitHub account and the repo you pushed to GitHub in module 4.

You will play both roles - PR author and reviewer - on your own repo, walking one full PR life cycle.

  1. Stand on the latest main, then create a branch for the change:
git switch main
git pull origin main
git switch -c practice/first-pr
  1. Make a small edit - add one line to the README - then commit:
echo "Practicing pull requests." >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "add a line to practice pull requests"
  1. Push the branch to GitHub:
git push -u origin practice/first-pr

  1. Open the repo in your browser: GitHub shows a yellow banner for the freshly pushed branch with a Compare & pull request button - click it (no banner? open the Pull requests tab → New pull request and pick practice/first-pr as compare). Fill in a title and a few description lines following the What/Why/How tested frame, then click Create pull request.

  2. Play the reviewer: open the Files changed tab and read the diff - the line you just added has a green background. Hover over that line, click the + that appears at its start, type a one-line comment (for example "reads fine"), and click Add single comment.

  3. Back on the Conversation tab, click Merge pull request (pick Squash and merge if the menu offers a choice) → Confirm. GitHub offers to delete the branch - click Delete branch.

  4. Back in the terminal, pull the main that now holds the change, and delete the local branch:

git switch main
git pull origin main
git branch -d practice/first-pr

Self-check:

  • git log --oneline -3 on main shows a new commit that came from the PR (with a squash merge the commit name carries the PR number, e.g. (#1)).
  • The PR page on GitHub shows the purple Merged badge, and your comment is still sitting on the Conversation tab.
  • git branch no longer lists practice/first-pr.

2. The life of a pull request
3. Review: reading the diff, commenting line by line

lessons.title: A team workflow feature branch → PR → main
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 30: A team workflow feature branch → PR → main

theory.contentHtml:
The last lesson explained what a PR is. This one fits it into a complete workflow - feature branch → PR → main - the frame that a data team of two or of twenty can use, and use almost identically.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Rule number one: main always works
  2. One task, one branch
  3. One full cycle
  4. Long-lived branches fall behind
  5. Two analysts, one repo
  6. Command reference
  7. Key points
  8. Practice on your machine

1. Rule number one: main always works

The whole workflow rests on a single promise: whoever checks out main, at any moment, gets a version that runs. The boss needs today's numbers? Clone main, run the pipeline, done. A new teammate joins? Clone main, everything works.

That promise only holds if nobody commits straight to main. A direct commit means a change nobody has read just became "the official version" - and the person who discovers it is broken will be whoever runs the report at 8 a.m.

Every change, even a one-line fix, takes the long way round: own branch → PR → review → merge. Many teams bolt the door with branch protection on GitHub - pushing straight to main is rejected. Not because they distrust each other, but so that bugs get stopped at the PR instead of discovered on main.

2. One task, one branch

Branches in this workflow are named after the task, not the person:

git switch -c an/fix-null-regions
  • an/fix-null-regions - who is doing it and what it is, readable from the name.
  • mai/add-cohort-chart - different task, different branch.

One branch = one task with an end point. When the task is done, the branch gets merged and deleted. Do not keep an an-dev branch alive for a month holding everything you do - a branch like that is never "done" enough to review, and the longer it lives the further it falls behind main (section 4).

Small tasks deserve a branch too. Creating one costs Git almost nothing - a branch is just a label pointing at a commit.

3. One full cycle

This is the rhythm you will repeat every day. Worth memorising:

# 1. Stand on the latest main
git switch main
git pull origin main

# 2. One branch for one task
git switch -c an/fix-null-regions

# 3. Work, then commit
git add clean_regions.py
git commit -m "map legacy region codes before grouping"

# 4. Push the branch and open a PR on GitHub
git push -u origin an/fix-null-regions

Then move to the browser: open the PR, wait for review, address feedback (commit + push to the same branch), and merge on GitHub. Once merged, return to the terminal to close the loop:

# 5. Back to main, take in what was just merged
git switch main
git pull origin main

# 6. The branch has served its purpose
git branch -d an/fix-null-regions

The two most commonly skipped steps are 5 and 6. Skip step 5 and your next branch starts from a stale main - missing the very change you just merged. Skip step 6 and the repo slowly becomes a graveyard of dead branches nobody can tell apart from live ones.

Note step 1: always start from the latest main. A branch carries the history of wherever it grew from - starting from a stale main is ordering conflicts for later.

4. Long-lived branches fall behind

While you work on your branch, main does not stand still - teammates' PRs get merged one after another. Your branch falls behind main: it grew from a point that keeps getting older.

A branch that lives 1–2 days is usually fine. A branch that lives a week should be brought back up to date, by merging main into it:

# While standing on your branch
git fetch origin
git merge origin/main

git fetch origin downloads the remote's latest state; git merge origin/main folds the new main into your branch. If there are conflicts, you resolve them on your own branch, at a time you choose - far better than letting them pile up until the moment you press merge on the PR. Once updated, your PR's diff shrinks back to only what you actually changed.

There is a second way, called rebase: instead of merging main in, it rewrites your commits as if you had branched off main today - a perfectly straight history, no merge commit in between. Rebase has its own safety rules (never rebase a branch others are using), so at this stage you only need to know it exists. Merging main into your branch is enough at this stage, but it can still produce conflicts or a broken integrated state. Run the tests and review the diff after the merge, before pushing.

5. Two analysts, one repo

Apply the frame to a two-person analytics team sharing one reporting repo:

  • An takes the revenue clean-up → branch an/revenue-cleanup, working in revenue_cleanup.ipynb.
  • Mai takes the churn analysis → branch mai/churn-cohorts, working in churn_cohorts.ipynb.

Each person has one notebook, one branch, one task. All week, nobody steps on anybody: An merges her PR Wednesday morning, Mai merges Thursday afternoon - Mai's branch needs one git merge origin/main to catch up, and because the two of them changed two different files, Git merges automatically; there is no conflict to resolve by hand.

Things only get messy when two people edit the same notebook. Conflicts inside an .ipynb file are far harder to untangle than in plain text (the next lesson explains why), so the pragmatic rule on data teams is: while someone is editing a notebook, the other person stays out of it - if you really must, talk first, or split the work into two files.

The workflow does not depend on team size. Two people or twenty, the frame stays: main is untouchable, one branch per task, everything goes through a PR.

Command reference

+-----------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|           Command           |                                          What it does                                         |
+-----------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| git switch main             | Return to the main branch                                                                     |
| git pull origin main        | Fetch and merge the latest main from the remote - the opening and closing step of every cycle |
| git switch -c <branch>      | Create a new branch for one task and switch to it                                             |
| git push -u origin <branch> | Push the branch to the remote for the first time, ready to open a PR                          |
| git fetch origin            | Download the remote's latest state (without merging anything yet)                             |
| git merge origin/main       | Fold the new main into the current branch - how a long-lived branch catches up                |
| git branch -d <branch>      | Delete a branch that has been merged                                                          |
+-----------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Key points

main is always in a working state. That is what the whole workflow serves. No direct commits to main - not even "it's just a one-line fix".

One task, one branch, started from the latest main. Branches are named after tasks, have an end point, and get deleted after merging.

When a branch falls behind, merge main into it. Resolve conflicts on home ground, at a time you choose. Rebase exists and makes prettier history, but you don't need it yet. Test after the merge: Git can combine text, but it cannot prove that the two changes work together.

Two people should not edit the same notebook. Different files merge themselves; the same .ipynb means conflicts that are painful to untangle - splitting work by file is the cheapest prevention.

Practice on your machine

This section needs a GitHub account and the repo you pushed to GitHub in module 4.

Run one full standard cycle end to end - the exact rhythm you will repeat every day on a team.

  1. Start from the latest main:
git switch main
git pull origin main
  1. Create a branch named after the task (keeping the name an is fine, or swap in your own name - just use it consistently in the later steps):
git switch -c an/add-notes-file
  1. Do the work, then commit - create a new notes file:
echo "workflow practice" > notes.md
git add notes.md
git commit -m "add notes file"
  1. Push the branch, then switch to the browser and open a PR (the Compare & pull request button), write a short description, and click Create pull request:
git push -u origin an/add-notes-file

  1. On the PR page, click Merge pull request → Confirm merge, then click Delete branch - the remote branch is deleted right there on the web.

  2. Back in the terminal, close the loop: pull the new main, delete the local branch, and prune the reference to the deleted remote branch:

git switch main
git pull origin main
git branch -d an/add-notes-file
git fetch --prune
  1. Survey the scene after the cycle:
git branch -a
git log --oneline -3

Self-check:

  • notes.md is on main after the pull - the loop is closed.
  • git branch -a no longer lists an/add-notes-file, locally or under remotes/origin/.
  • git log --oneline -3 shows this cycle's commit sitting on main.

lessons.title: Notebooks and large data in Git
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 32: Notebooks and large data in Git

theory.contentHtml:
Git was built for code: small text files, a few changed lines at a time. Data projects throw at it the two things it tolerates worst - notebooks and large data files. This lesson shows why they hurt, and the discipline for living with them.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Why notebooks hurt in Git
  2. Notebook discipline
  3. Why large data files are even worse
  4. Code in Git, data outside
  5. Git LFS and DVC
  6. Decision table: commit, ignore, or LFS
  7. Command reference
  8. Key points
  9. Practice on your machine

1. Why notebooks hurt in Git

Open an .ipynb file in a text editor (not Jupyter) and you will see it is really JSON:

{
  "cell_type": "code",
  "execution_count": 12,
  "source": ["df.plot()"],
  "outputs": [{
    "data": {
      "image/png": "iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAABkAAAAPeCAYAAAD..."
    }
  }]
}

That iVBORw0KGgo... string is the entire chart image, base64-encoded, sitting inside the file - typically thousands of "lines" long. And that is just one cell.

Two consequences:

  • Shredded diffs. Merely re-running the notebook - without editing a character of code - changes execution_count, outputs and metadata. The PR diff balloons by hundreds of junk lines, burying the few lines of code that actually changed. The reviewer gives up.
  • Miserable conflicts. Two people run the same notebook and merge: Git sees two different JSON versions and makes you resolve the conflict by hand, inside a thousand-line JSON file - where one misplaced comma means the notebook no longer opens.

2. Notebook discipline

Discipline number one, the cheapest and most effective: clear outputs before committing.

In Jupyter: Kernel → Restart & Clear Output. Picking the Restart variant rather than just Clear is deliberate: restarting also kills the old variables in memory, so if your notebook secretly depends on a variable created by a deleted cell, you find out right now - instead of a colleague finding out when they run it from the top.

From the command line (handy for many files):

jupyter nbconvert --clear-output --inplace churn_cohorts.ipynb

After clearing, the .ipynb file holds only code and markdown - the diff is readable, and conflicts become rare and fixable.

Discipline number two: stable logic gradually moves into .py files. Data-cleaning functions, metric formulas - anything used repeatedly - becomes a module imported into the notebook. The notebook keeps its true job: exploring and presenting. The .py file is plain text, and Git handles it beautifully.

For anyone who wants properly civilised notebook diffs: nbdime diffs and merges cell by cell instead of line by JSON-line; ReviewNB renders notebooks right inside GitHub PRs. Know the names so you can look them up - the clear-output discipline remains the foundation.

3. Why large data files are even worse

Notebooks make ugly diffs; large data files damage the whole repo, permanently. The root is a property you already know: Git keeps EVERY version of every file, forever - its great strength with code, and a death sentence with data.

Commit a 500MB sales.csv, then update it 10 times? The repo now carries a dozen versions. Every git clone from now on downloads that entire history - the new teammate's laptop, and CI if you have it, pay the price every time.

Worse: deleting the file and committing does not reclaim the space - the file still lives in the old commits, and clones still download all of it. History is the thing Git does not let you casually edit (the next lesson meets this property again somewhere far more painful: leaked passwords).

GitHub also steps in before you do: files over 100MB are rejected at push, over 50MB triggers a warning. But do not read 100MB as "so 99MB is fine" - a 99MB file that changes often is still a disaster for the repo.

4. Code in Git, data outside

The principle in one sentence: Git keeps the code, somewhere else keeps the data.

  • Data lives where data belongs: object storage (S3, Google Cloud Storage), Google Drive, a database, a data warehouse.
  • The repo holds a download script - anyone who clones can rebuild the data:
python scripts/download_data.py
  • The README names the source: where the data lives, how to request access, which command downloads it.

And the safety latch so nobody slips: ignore the data folder from day one. Add to .gitignore:

data/
*.parquet

From now on git status never lists files under data/ - committing them by accident becomes hard.

The one reasonable exception: tiny sample files (a few KB, a few dozen rows) used as documentation examples or test fixtures - those can be committed, because in the broader sense they are part of the code.

5. Git LFS and DVC

Git LFS (Large File Storage) is the halfway answer for big files that must travel with the repo. The mechanism: inside the repo, Git stores only a few-line pointer file (hash and size); the real file lives in a separate store alongside. On clone, LFS fetches the latest real file - the repo's history never balloons.

git lfs install
git lfs track "*.pkl"
git add .gitattributes model.pkl
git commit -m "track model files with LFS"

git lfs track writes the rule into .gitattributes - a file that must be committed so the whole team shares the rule. LFS suits mid-sized binaries that need to be versioned with the code: a model of a few dozen MB, design assets. It does not rescue a repo that has already ballooned - pointers only apply to new commits.

And when you need real data versioning - "which data version produced this result?", multi-GB datasets, your own remote storage - there is a dedicated tool: DVC (Data Version Control), built on top of Git with the same pointer philosophy but for whole datasets and pipelines. At this course's level, knowing the name and when to reach for it is enough.

6. Decision table: commit, ignore, or LFS

Pin this next to your screen:

+----------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                         File type                        |                   What to do                   |                                Why                                |
+----------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Code: .py, .sql, .R                                      | Commit                                         | Plain text, clean diffs - exactly Git's dish                      |
| .ipynb notebook with outputs cleared                     | Commit                                         | What remains is code + markdown, which Git handles                |
| Tiny sample files (a few KB) for tests/examples          | Commit                                         | They are part of the code                                         |
| Real CSV/Parquet data                                    | Ignore - keep in S3/Drive/DB + download script | Git keeps every version forever; GitHub blocks >100MB             |
| Mid-sized models/binaries that must travel with the repo | Git LFS                                        | The repo keeps a pointer; the real file lives in a separate store |
| Data needing true versioning, many GB                    | DVC (look it up when needed)                   | Versions datasets + pipelines, beyond LFS's reach                 |
| .env, credentials                                        | NEVER commit                                   | Next lesson - important enough to get a lesson of its own         |
+----------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------+

Command reference

+---------------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                      Command                      |                                         What it does                                         |
+---------------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| jupyter nbconvert --clear-output --inplace <file> | Strip all notebook outputs in place - run before committing                                  |
| git rm --cached <file>                            | Stop tracking a file while keeping it on disk - for when a data file got tracked by mistake  |
| git lfs install                                   | Enable Git LFS on this machine (once)                                                        |
| git lfs track "*.pkl"                             | Register a file pattern to go through LFS - written to .gitattributes, remember to commit it |
| nbdiff a.ipynb b.ipynb                            | Diff two notebooks cell by cell (nbdime tool) instead of by JSON line                        |
+---------------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Key points

A notebook is JSON that contains its outputs. Re-running changes the diff even when the code didn't change - clearing outputs before committing (Kernel → Restart & Clear Output) is the cheapest, most effective discipline in this whole lesson.

Git keeps every version forever - so keep large data out. Deleting a file doesn't reclaim space; GitHub blocks files over 100MB. Code goes in Git; data lives in S3/Drive/DB with a download script + a README naming the source.

Git LFS = a pointer in the repo, the real file in a separate store. For binaries that must travel with the repo; it cannot rescue one that already ballooned.

Stable logic moves into .py. Notebooks are for exploring and presenting; reusable functions belong in modules - clean diffs, reviewable code.

Practice on your machine

This section is entirely local - use the practice repo you already have from the previous modules, or a fresh one created with git init.

You will produce a shredded notebook diff with your own hands, watch it turn clean after clearing outputs - then install the safety latch for large data files.

  1. Create a fake notebook - a JSON file shaped like an .ipynb, carrying long outputs that mimic a base64 image - then commit it:
cat > fake.ipynb << 'EOF'
{
 "cells": [{
  "cell_type": "code",
  "execution_count": 1,
  "source": ["df.plot()"],
  "outputs": [{"data": {"image/png": [
   "iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAABkAAAAPeCAYAAADtvzO6AAAAOXRFWHRTb2Z0d2FyZQBN",
   "YXRwbG90bGliIHZlcnNpb24zLjguMiwgaHR0cHM6Ly9tYXRwbG90bGliLm9yZy8g4bPq",
   "AAAACXBIWXMAAA9hAAAPYQGoP6dpAAEAAElEQVR4nOzdeVxU9f4G8OfMDMO+72Cu",
   "uOWWmVmapVbXzKxbt1u3fbe63bJ9sX1fbLfFyjRzS3PLXcENFGSHYd+3Yd9nn+f3",
   "B78hEFDWmTnnfN6vly9l5pwz3+c5Z85nznfmnMMwDMMwDMMwDMMwDMMwDMMwDMOI",
   "Bp/rABiGYRiGYRiGYRiGYRiGYRiGYbSFFUgYhmEYhmEYhmEYhmEYhmEYhhENViBh",
   "GIZhGIZhGIZhGIZhGIZhGEY0WIGEYRiGYRiGYRiGYRiGYRiGYRjRYAUShmEYhmEY",
   "hmEYhmEYhmEYhmEY0WAFEoZhGIZhGIZhGIZhGIZhGIZhRIMVSBiGYRiGYRiGYRiG"
  ]}}]
 }]
}
EOF
git add fake.ipynb
git commit -m "add fake notebook with long outputs"

  1. Simulate re-running the notebook: open fake.ipynb in a text editor, change "execution_count": 1 to 7 and scramble a few characters in 2–3 of the long string lines (exactly what happens when a cell re-runs: the generated output comes out different). Save the file - note that the code line df.plot() did not change by a single character.

  2. Look at the diff:

git diff fake.ipynb

Every change is output and metadata - exactly the kind of junk that buries code in a real PR.

  1. "Clear outputs": overwrite with the clean version and commit:
cat > fake.ipynb << 'EOF'
{
 "cells": [{
  "cell_type": "code",
  "execution_count": null,
  "source": ["df.plot()"],
  "outputs": []
 }]
}
EOF
git add fake.ipynb
git commit -m "clear notebook outputs"
  1. Now change the actual code: open the editor, change df.plot() to df.plot(kind="bar"), save, and diff again:
git diff fake.ipynb

This time the diff is exactly one source line - a reviewer reads it in a second.

  1. Install the safety latch for large data: create a big file under data/raw/ and ignore the whole folder:
mkdir -p data/raw
seq 1 200000 > data/raw/big.csv
echo "data/" >> .gitignore
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "ignore data directory"
  1. Confirm Git truly looks away from that file:
git status
git check-ignore -v data/raw/big.csv

Self-check:

  • The diff in step 3 is packed with base64 string lines even though you changed no character of code.
  • The diff in step 5 is a single source line - same file, different discipline.
  • git status says nothing about data/raw/big.csv, and git check-ignore -v points at exactly the data/ rule in .gitignore.

lessons.title: Keeping secrets out .env, keys, and the cure
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 33: Keeping secrets out .env, keys, and the cure

theory.contentHtml:
Sooner or later, someone on the team pastes an API key into a notebook "just to get it running" - and pushes. This lesson is so that person isn't you, and so that when it does happen, you know which step comes before which.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. The classic accident
  2. Prevention: .env and environment variables
  3. .gitignore from the moment the repo is born
  4. Already pushed: rotate the key first
  5. Cleaning history: git filter-repo
  6. GitHub guards the door too
  7. Command reference
  8. Key points
  9. Practice on your machine

1. The classic accident

It always starts innocently - a notebook cell fetching weather data:

# somewhere in a notebook cell
api_key = "sk-live-9f8e7d6c5b4a3f2e1d0c"
weather = fetch_weather("Hanoi", api_key)

The notebook gets committed and pushed to a public GitHub repo. What happens next is not "maybe nobody will notice": there are bots scanning GitHub 24/7, watching the stream of new commits in real time, running regexes for each provider's exact key format (AWS, OpenAI, Google, Stripe...). A key exposed in a public repo is found and used within minutes - not days. The familiar script: an AWS key leaks in the evening; by morning the account has a bill for thousands of dollars of coin-mining compute.

A private repo is safer, but do not call it safe: a key sitting in history is a time bomb - waiting for the day the repo goes public, gains a collaborator, or a stray clone lingers on someone's laptop.

Database passwords share the same fate: a connection string like mysql://user:password@host written straight into code is a password stored in Git.

2. Prevention: .env and environment variables

The standard prevention, used in every language: secrets leave the code and move into a .env file - a small text file at the project root, one variable per line:

OPENWEATHER_API_KEY=sk-live-9f8e7d6c5b4a3f2e1d0c
DB_PASSWORD=s3cret-pa55

The code no longer contains the value - it reads it through an environment variable, along these lines:

import os

api_key = os.environ["OPENWEATHER_API_KEY"]
weather = fetch_weather("Hanoi", api_key)

The code now says "I need a key called OPENWEATHER_API_KEY" without saying what the key is. The real value sits in .env on your machine - each teammate has their own .env with their own keys. (Libraries like python-dotenv load .env into the environment at runtime - a name worth knowing.)

Once separated, the code can be pushed freely - the one thing that must never be pushed is .env. That is the next section's job.

3. .gitignore from the moment the repo is born

The .env line must go into .gitignore at repo creation, before the first commit:

echo ".env" >> .gitignore
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "ignore .env"

Why "at creation"? Two reasons:

  • .gitignore only blocks files that are not yet tracked. Commit .env once and add the ignore rule afterwards - too late; it is already in history.
  • "I'll do it later" discipline does not exist. Every repo starts with "just temporarily".

But if .env is ignored, how does a new teammate know which variables they need? The answer is a second file - .env.example - committed to the repo, containing variable names but no values:

OPENWEATHER_API_KEY=
DB_PASSWORD=

The newcomer clones, copies .env.example to .env, and fills in their own keys. The structure is shared; the secrets are not.

4. Already pushed: rotate the key first

Now the cure. Almost everyone's first reflex is to delete the file and push immediately:

git rm --cached .env
git commit -m "remove .env from repo"
git push

Not enough - and worse, it creates a false sense of safety. The new commit only says "from now on this file is gone"; every old commit keeps its content untouched. See for yourself:

git log --all --oneline -- .env

Output:

9c1e2f0 remove .env from repo
4b7a8d3 add weather pipeline config

The history is still there, and git show 4b7a8d3:.env prints the key just fine. Anyone who clones the repo can read it.

So the step that is MANDATORY and comes FIRST is not a Git step at all: revoke or rotate the key at the provider, immediately - open the dashboard, revoke the old key, issue a new one. Engrave the principle: a leaked key is a lost key, no matter how fast you delete - bots read commits faster than you can type the delete command, and their caches have no undo button.

Once rotated, the system is safe again even though Git history still holds the dead key. Everything after that is just cleanup.

5. Cleaning history: git filter-repo

To make the dead key vanish from history entirely (fewer false alarms, fewer awkward audit questions), you need a tool that rewrites history. The tool the Git documentation itself recommends today: git filter-repo (installed separately; not bundled with Git).

git filter-repo --invert-paths --path .env

This walks the entire history and rebuilds every commit as if .env had never existed.

But rewriting history is the whole team's affair, not one person's:

  • Every commit from that point on changes its hash - the new history and the old one are two different timelines.
  • Every teammate's clone still holds the old timeline → after the new history is force-pushed, everyone must re-clone (or hard-reset following instructions), or their next push brings the key right back.

So: tell the team, pick a moment, do it once and cleanly. And remember the order - filter-repo is step two; step one is still rotation, because cleaning your history does not erase the copies in the bots' hands.

6. GitHub guards the door too

GitHub has two safety nets for exactly this accident. Secret scanning sweeps repos for known key formats - when it finds one it alerts you, and many key types are reported straight to the provider for automatic revocation. Push protection goes further: it blocks the push on the spot when a commit appears to contain a secret - the key never even touches GitHub. It is free on public repos; check that it is enabled in your team repo's Settings.

A safety net is a safety net: it catches known key formats, not a homemade password like quan-trong-123. The .env + .gitignore + .env.example discipline remains the main line of defence.

Command reference

+----------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                    Command                   |                                                  What it does                                                  |
+----------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| echo ".env" >> .gitignore                    | Add .env to the ignore list - do it the moment the repo is created                                             |
| git check-ignore -v .env                     | Check whether a file is ignored, and by which rule                                                             |
| git rm --cached .env                         | Untrack the file in new commits (it stays on disk) - does not erase history                                    |
| git log --all --oneline -- <file>            | List every commit that ever touched a file - how to check whether a key is still in history                    |
| git filter-repo --invert-paths --path <file> | Rewrite the entire history, removing a file from every commit - installed separately, coordinate with the team |
+----------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Key points

A leaked key is a lost key. The first, mandatory, non-negotiable step: rotate the key at the provider. Bots read commits within minutes - deleting the file cannot win that race.

Deleting the file + a new commit does NOT erase history. git log --all -- .env shows you the truth. Cleaning history takes git filter-repo - and that is step two, after rotation.

Prevention is a hundred times cheaper than the cure: secrets go in .env, code reads environment variables, .env goes into .gitignore at repo creation, and a committed .env.example carries variable names without values.

Rewriting history is a whole-team affair. Every hash changes and everyone must re-clone - announce it first, do it once and cleanly.

Practice on your machine

This section is entirely local and uses a fake key from start to finish - never repeat the experiment with a real key.

You will build the standard .env line of defence, then stage the "accident" on purpose to see with your own eyes why deleting a file cannot rescue a committed key.

  1. Create a fake .env file:
echo "FAKE_API_KEY=sk-test-0000-not-a-real-key" > .env
  1. Block it immediately with .gitignore, then verify with Git's own tool:
echo ".env" >> .gitignore
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "ignore .env"
git check-ignore -v .env

git check-ignore -v prints which rule in which file is blocking .env - and from now on git status never mentions it.

  1. Create .env.example - the committable version, carrying variable names but no values:
echo "FAKE_API_KEY=" > .env.example
git add .env.example
git commit -m "add .env.example"
  1. Now restage the classic accident - deliberately "slip" and commit a fake secret file:
echo "FAKE_API_KEY=sk-test-0000-not-a-real-key" > secret.txt
git add secret.txt
git commit -m "add config file"
  1. The common reflex: delete the file, make a new commit, assume it is over:
git rm secret.txt
git commit -m "remove secret file"
  1. Verify the lesson's warning yourself - history still holds everything:
git log --all --oneline -- secret.txt

Two lines appear: the deleting commit and the "accident" commit. Take the hash on the LOWER line (the add config file commit), and read the deleted file's content back:

git show <hash>:secret.txt

(replace <hash> with the hash you just saw.) The FAKE_API_KEY content prints out intact - the "deleted" file is still readable from history. This is exactly why the first move after leaking a real key is rotating it at the provider, not deleting the file.

Self-check:

  • git check-ignore -v .env points at the .env rule in .gitignore, and git status does not list .env.
  • .env.example is in a commit and carries variable names only.
  • git show <hash>:secret.txt prints the fake key even though the file is gone from disk - you have seen with your own eyes why "delete and commit" cannot rescue a leaked key.
  • Start to finish there was only the fake key sk-test-0000-not-a-real-key - no real key ever touched the repo.

4. Already pushed: rotate the key first
