questions.prompt: Is a pull request a Git command or a GitHub feature?

options.label: A
options.text: A git command - you type git pull-request to open one

options.label: B
options.text: A GitHub feature, built on top of Git's branch concept

options.label: C
options.text: Another name for the git pull command

options.label: D
options.text: A special kind of commit that Git creates

questions.explanation: Git provides branches and merging; the 'propose - discuss - approve - press merge' part is a feature of the hosting platform (GitHub; GitLab calls it a merge request). Typing git pull-request gets you an immediate 'not a git command' error - no such command exists, so option a is wrong. Option c is a treacherous mix-up: git pull is the command that FETCHES changes from the remote to your machine, and has nothing to do with proposing a merge - the word 'pull' overlaps because a PR literally means 'please pull my branch into main'. Option d is wrong because a PR is not a kind of commit - it is a proposal with a diff and a discussion space; only when the merge button is pressed does a commit (a merge commit or a squash commit) appear on main.

questions.prompt: Why does the team workflow forbid committing straight to main?

options.label: A
options.text: Because Git technically does not allow commits on main

options.label: B
options.text: Because main must always be in a working state - every change must be read via a PR before it lands

options.label: C
options.text: Because committing straight to main erases the history of other branches

options.label: D
options.text: Because only the team lead is allowed to create commits on main

questions.explanation: The whole workflow rests on one promise: whoever checks out main, at any time, gets a version that runs. A direct commit means a change nobody has read just became 'the official version' - the bug gets discovered by whoever runs the report, instead of being stopped at the PR. Option a is wrong: plain Git forbids nothing - main is a branch like any other; the ban is a team convention (which can be enforced with branch protection on GitHub, but that is GitHub, not Git). Option c is wrong because committing to main touches no other branch's history. Option d is wrong: the rule applies to everyone including the lead - the lead's code needs another reader just as much.

questions.prompt: The project needs a 2GB sales.csv file. What is the right way to handle it?

options.label: A
options.text: Commit it straight into the repo so everyone who clones has it

options.label: B
options.text: Zip it to make it smaller, then commit

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the file outside Git (S3/Drive/DB), commit a download script + a README naming the source, and ignore the data file

options.label: D
options.text: Split it into several files under 100MB and commit the parts

questions.explanation: The principle: code in Git, data outside. The repo carries a download script + a README naming the source, so anyone who clones can still rebuild the data - achieving the 'everyone has it' goal without wrecking the repo. Option a fails twice: GitHub rejects files over 100MB at push, and even if you got around that, Git keeps EVERY version forever - a few updates and the repo balloons irreversibly; deleting the file doesn't help because history remains. Option b changes nothing fundamental: a zip of 2GB of data is still a giant file over the limit, and worse, it's compressed binary - every data change makes the repo carry one more full zip. Option d dodges the 100MB check but keeps the real killer: 2GB × every version sits in history forever, and every clone downloads all of it.

questions.prompt: You accidentally pushed a notebook containing an API key to a public repo. What is the FIRST thing to do?

options.label: A
options.text: Delete the key from the notebook, commit and push immediately

options.label: B
options.text: Revoke/rotate the key at the provider right away - a leaked key is a lost key

options.label: C
options.text: Switch the repo to private so nobody can see it anymore

options.label: D
options.text: Run git filter-repo to remove the key from the whole history

questions.explanation: Bots scan GitHub 24/7, watching new commits in real time - a key in a public repo gets used within minutes. That makes every repo-side action a treatment of symptoms: only rotating the key at the provider actually disables what leaked, and once rotated the system is safe again even though history still holds the dead key. Option a is the most dangerous because it creates false safety: the deleting commit only says 'gone from now on', every old commit still holds the key (git log --all -- <file> proves it), and the bots may have finished reading before you typed the delete. Option c cannot claw back what bots cached while the repo was public. Option d is WORTH doing but is step TWO - cleaning your history does not erase the copies in other people's hands, so the question 'what comes first' has only one answer.

questions.prompt: Why should notebook outputs be cleared before committing?

options.label: A
options.text: Because outputs make the notebook slower to open next time

options.label: B
options.text: Because outputs (tables, base64 images) live inside the JSON - a re-run floods the diff with noise even when the code didn't change, and conflicts inside outputs are brutal to untangle

options.label: C
options.text: Because GitHub cannot display a notebook that still has outputs

options.label: D
options.text: Because Git refuses to commit a notebook file containing outputs

questions.explanation: An .ipynb file is JSON that contains its outputs - including entire chart images base64-encoded across thousands of lines. Merely re-running the notebook, without touching a character of code, changes execution_count and outputs → the PR diff balloons with junk, burying the few lines that really changed; two people running the same notebook and merging means a conflict inside thousand-line JSON, where hand-editing easily corrupts the file. Clearing outputs (Kernel → Restart & Clear Output) reduces the notebook to what deserves versioning: code and markdown. Option a is wrong - outputs make the file somewhat heavier but that is not the reason; option c is wrong because GitHub renders notebooks with outputs just fine (many people like viewing them); option d is wrong because Git refuses nothing - it commits obediently, which is precisely why the discipline has to come from humans.

questions.prompt:
You accidentally committed secret.txt containing an API key, then deleted the file and made a new commit. Checking again:


$ git log --all --oneline -- secret.txt
8f3c2a1 remove secret file
5d9e0b7 add config file


Reading this output, which conclusion is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The file is gone from history - git show 5d9e0b7:secret.txt will error because the deleting commit comes after it

options.label: B
options.text: The content of secret.txt is still readable from commit 5d9e0b7 - if the key were real, it must be rotated at the provider right away; cleaning history is only a later step

options.label: C
options.text: Commit 8f3c2a1 overwrote commit 5d9e0b7, so the repo now keeps only the version without the file

options.label: D
options.text: Adding secret.txt to .gitignore is enough to make the old content in history unreadable

questions.explanation: The very fact that git log --all still lists TWO commits is the proof: history keeps both the 'accident' commit and the deleting commit. git show 5d9e0b7:secret.txt prints the key content just fine - the deleting commit only says 'from this point on the file is gone' and touches nothing that came before it, so option a is wrong. Option c is wrong at the same root: a commit never overwrites a commit - each one is an immutable snapshot and new commits only append to the chain; if 8f3c2a1 had really overwritten anything, git log could not have printed the 5d9e0b7 line. Option d mistakes .gitignore's role: it only stops UNTRACKED files from being added in the future, and has zero effect on content already sitting inside commits. Option b is right on both counts: the content is intact in history, and since bots may have finished reading before you deleted, the first move with a real key is always rotation at the provider - git filter-repo is only the second, cleanup step.

questions.prompt:
You are asked to review a PR. Running git diff --stat against the PR's branch shows:


$ git diff --stat origin/main
 analysis/eda_customers.ipynb | 18422 ++++++++++++++++--------------
 analysis/eda_orders.ipynb    | 12907 ++++++++++---------
 analysis/eda_products.ipynb  |  9310 ++++++------
 ...
 src/clean_regions.py         |    28 ++++++++++++++-
 README.md                    |     4 ++++
 40 files changed, 96219 insertions(+), 84152 deletions(-)


38 of the 40 files are notebooks, each with thousands of changed lines that are all output (result tables, base64 images); the real code change lives in clean_regions.py. What is the reviewer's correct move?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve right away - nearly a hundred thousand changed lines prove the author worked very hard

options.label: B
options.text: Read all 40 files in order to be fair, a few files a day, and approve once done

options.label: C
options.text: Request changes: ask the author to clear the notebook outputs (and consider moving reusable logic into .py files), then push to the same branch - the diff shrinks back to the real code worth reading

options.label: D
options.text: Tell the author to close the PR, commit the notebook part straight to main to keep things tidy, and open a new PR only for clean_regions.py

questions.explanation: The 96 thousand inserted lines here are not effort - they are notebook output: re-running cells makes result tables and base64 images come out different, so the diff balloons even though the logic did not change. Option c fixes the root: clearing outputs reduces the notebooks to code + markdown, the diff shrinks to exactly what the reviewer needs to read, and because the push goes to the SAME branch the PR updates itself - the old discussion stays, no new PR needed. Option a is wrong because diff size does not measure effort, and approving what you cannot read is precisely the 'LGTM' the lesson warns about - review becomes a formality. Option b sounds diligent but is useless: those 38 files are auto-generated junk, and reading them tells you nothing about the data transformation logic - the problem is in the diff, not in the reader's stamina. Option d breaks rule number one of the team workflow: no direct commits to main - 38 notebooks nobody has read landing straight on main makes the review gate meaningless; the right direction is making the diff readable, not sneaking around the review.
